title: Upper and lower limbs — anatomy and related sciences
scopeNote: Both limbs are in scope per the user’s exam confirmation. Existing anatomy follows the local Gray’s Student checklist and available upper-limb transcripts. New regional detail is checked against cited Gray’s 42nd-edition pages, with related limb development, histology and muscle physiology from Langman, Junqueira and Guyton. Missing lower-limb/later-hand teacher material and unconfirmed related-science lecture detail remain book extensions. Source links sample objectives, not every paragraph or official exam weighting; genuine past papers remain separate.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Shoulder suspension, capsule and stabilizers
modules.description: Shoulder stability depends on specific suspensory ligaments, cuff compression and capsular reinforcements. Joint cavities and adjacent bursae define routes for fluid spread.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Branch-level localization in the shoulder and arm
modules.description: Selective muscle testing localizes a lesion along the brachial plexus or a terminal nerve. A lesion distal to an early motor branch can spare that muscle while affecting more distal targets.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Elbow stability and forearm load transfer
modules.description: The radius and ulna function as a linked unit. The radial head, interosseous membrane and distal radioulnar stabilizers share longitudinal loads, while collateral ligaments control angular instability.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Forearm vessels and nerve relationships
modules.description: Recurrent arteries reconnect distal vessels to the brachial system around the elbow. Fascial openings and muscle heads guide nerves into compartments and explain selective deficits.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Finger and thumb tendon mechanics
modules.description: The extensor expansion, volar plates and flexor pulleys couple motion across finger joints. Their failure produces distinct deformities even when the main muscle and nerve remain intact.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Hand nerve branches, arches and tendon sheaths
modules.description: Hand symptoms depend on whether a lesion affects proximal or distal branches, and infections follow specific synovial sheaths. Palmar arches and tendon nutrient folds occupy different depths.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Hip capsule, cartilage and communicating spaces
modules.description: The capsule has asymmetric femoral attachments and contains the capital growth plate. The acetabular articular ring, central fossa and adjacent bursae explain loading and fluid distribution.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Thigh circulation and changing neurovascular planes
modules.description: The profunda femoris and its perforating branches form longitudinal collateral channels, while the femoral vein changes sides along the artery. Superficial venous and cutaneous nerve routes explain selective procedural deficits.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Knee recesses, stabilizers and load-bearing mechanics
modules.description: Knee fluid follows synovial recesses, while flexion changes cruciate tension, patellar restraint and the muscular work required to support body weight.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Localizing leg nerve lesions by spared functions
modules.description: Distinguish nerve injury levels by combining cutaneous loss with motor functions supplied before and after the suspected lesion.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Ankle mortise, tendon restraints and surgical relations
modules.description: The ankle mortise accommodates the asymmetric talar trochlea; retinacula restrain tendons along different routes from the collateral ligaments.

modules.subject: anatomy
modules.title: Foot arches, intrinsic mechanics and deep circulation
modules.description: Passive fascial tension and intrinsic muscle lines of pull shape the foot as a lever, while plantar nerve branches and vascular arches occupy distinct tissue planes.

modules.subject: embryology
modules.title: Limb growth, compartment innervation and developmental disruptions
modules.description: Limb elongation, muscle innervation and congenital deformities arise through different developmental processes. Distinguishing loss of growth, altered pattern and reduced fetal movement clarifies otherwise similar limb findings.

modules.subject: histology
modules.title: Cartilage resilience and bone mechanobiology
modules.description: Limb tissues share connective-tissue ancestry but have distinct nutrient routes and mechanical components. Cartilage hydration, osteocyte sensing and osteoclast resorption explain functional and disease patterns.

modules.subject: histology
modules.title: Muscle force transmission, excitation architecture and repair
modules.description: A skeletal muscle is a mechanically continuous tissue whose fibers transmit force through collagen. Sarcomeric accessory proteins, triads and satellite cells solve distinct structural problems.

modules.subject: physiology
modules.title: Skeletal-muscle length, load, activation and relaxation
modules.description: Separating active from passive tension, force from shortening, and electrical excitation from calcium handling explains muscle behavior under experimental and limb-loading conditions.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Upper-limb functional design and regional orientation
concepts.summary: The upper limb uses coordinated girdle, shoulder, elbow, radioulnar, wrist and digital movement to position the hand as a mechanically versatile and highly sensory end organ.
keyPoints: The sternoclavicular joint is the only direct bony articulation between upper limb and axial skeleton.
Scapular motion on the thoracic wall enlarges the range available at the glenohumeral joint.
Elbow flexion-extension and forearm pronation-supination position the palm without requiring shoulder rotation alone.
Dense sensory innervation and opposable thumb support precision handling as well as power grip.
examTraps: The scapulothoracic articulation is functional, not a true synovial joint.
Thumb is lateral in anatomical position even though it appears medial in some rotated images.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the central functional theme of upper-limb organization?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Coordinated serial joints position a versatile, highly sensory hand for power and precision tasks.

objectives.text: Identify the sternoclavicular joint as the upper limb's only direct bony articulation with the axial skeleton.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Upper-limb surface anatomy and integrated clinical localization
concepts.summary: Surface landmarks connect the deep anatomy of axilla, arm, cubital fossa, distal forearm and hand to examination. A safe interpretation uses a known tendon or bone before inferring a nearby nerve or vessel.
keyPoints: Axillary contents are projected from the apex into the upper arm around the humerus and pectoral folds.
Brachial pulse is medial to biceps tendon; cubital fossa order protects the artery and median nerve beneath the aponeurosis.
Radial pulse is lateral to FCR tendon; ulnar bundle is lateral to FCU tendon.
Motor testing separates median thenar opposition, ulnar interosseous ab/adduction and radial wrist/finger extension.
examTraps: A palpable surface landmark is not itself proof of an intact deep nerve; combine motor, sensory and relation findings.
Gray's surface-anatomy section ends on printed p. 828; the clinical cases on pp. 829-834 are separately inventoried anatomical applications.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which three quick movements broadly sample terminal motor nerves in the hand?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Thumb opposition for median, finger abduction/adduction for ulnar, and wrist/finger extension for radial nerve.

objectives.text: Select resisted finger abduction as a motor test of the deep ulnar nerve in the hand.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Lower-limb surface anatomy and integrated clinical localization
concepts.summary: Surface anatomy links femoral and popliteal pulses, knee landmarks, ankle tendons, tarsal tunnel, dorsalis pedis and superficial veins to the regional map. These are anatomical localization aids rather than procedural guidance.
keyPoints: Femoral artery is found below the inguinal ligament between ASIS and pubic symphysis region; femoral nerve is lateral and vein medial.
Popliteal pulse is deep and best sought with knee flexed to relax hamstrings and gastrocnemius.
Posterior tibial pulse is behind medial malleolus; dorsalis pedis is lateral to EHL tendon.
Great saphenous is anterior to medial malleolus; small saphenous is posterior to lateral malleolus.
examTraps: Pulse absence has clinical differential diagnoses beyond anatomy and is not alone proof of occlusion at the palpation site.
Gray's surface-anatomy section ends on printed p. 671; the clinical cases on pp. 672-681 are separately inventoried anatomical applications.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Pair the two foot pulses with landmarks.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Posterior tibial behind medial malleolus; dorsalis pedis lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon.

objectives.text: Locate the dorsalis pedis pulse relative to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Osteological language and limb skeleton
concepts.summary: Bone-surface vocabulary is a decoding system: elevations indicate attachments, smooth cartilage-covered areas indicate articulations, grooves/notches transmit structures, and the free upper limb is oriented relative to the pectoral girdle.
keyPoints: Linear elevations are described as lines or crests; rounded projections include tubercles and tuberosities; sharp projections include spines and processes.
Fossae and grooves are depressions, whereas foramina and canals are passages; naming the feature predicts what may attach or pass.
The pectoral girdle is clavicle plus scapula; humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges form the free limb.
The thumb is lateral in anatomical position, a convention needed before applying radial and ulnar relations.
examTraps: A cartilage-covered facet is an articular surface, not a muscle-attachment roughening.
Do not use palmar/dorsal orientation before first establishing anatomical position.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does a bony groove most often tell you?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It marks a channel for a tendon, vessel or nerve, or a linear attachment; its regional relations determine which.

objectives.text: Recognize a fossa as a depression in osteological terminology.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Clavicle orientation, attachments and fracture
concepts.summary: The clavicle is a subcutaneous horizontal strut between sternum and acromion. Its curves, ends and inferior markings permit reliable siding and explain its common fracture pattern and fragment displacement.
keyPoints: The enlarged sternal end is medial; the flattened acromial end is lateral.
The medial two thirds are convex anteriorly and the lateral third concave anteriorly; the subclavian groove faces inferiorly.
The conoid tubercle and trapezoid line anchor the coracoclavicular ligament laterally, while the costoclavicular impression is medial.
The junction of medial two thirds and lateral third is a common fracture site; muscle pull and limb weight displace fragments in different directions.
examTraps: The conoid tubercle is inferior and posterolateral, not a superior palpable landmark.
A clavicle fracture question may test displacement rather than merely the common site.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do you side an isolated clavicle?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Put the bulky sternal end medially, the flat acromial end laterally, the shaft's medial convexity anteriorly, and the subclavian groove inferiorly.

objectives.text: Orient the clavicle using its inferior-surface landmarks.
Identify the common site of clavicular fracture.
Match clavicular ends to their articulations.
Identify the clavicle in a rotatable upper-limb model.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Scapular surfaces, borders, processes and attachments
concepts.summary: The triangular scapula is oriented by its posterior spine and lateral glenoid cavity. Fossae, processes, borders and notches organize muscle attachment, joint formation and neurovascular passage.
keyPoints: The spine divides the posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and expands laterally into the acromion.
The costal surface is the subscapular fossa; the thick lateral border leads to the glenoid cavity.
The coracoid anchors short-head biceps, coracobrachialis, pectoralis minor and several stabilizing ligaments.
The suprascapular notch is bridged by the superior transverse scapular ligament; the suprascapular nerve passes through the resulting foramen.
examTraps: The suprascapular artery usually passes over the superior transverse scapular ligament while the nerve passes under it.
The glenoid cavity faces laterally, not directly anteriorly.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which landmarks distinguish the anterior and posterior scapular surfaces?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The smooth subscapular fossa marks the anterior surface; the spine with supra- and infraspinous fossae marks the posterior surface.

objectives.text: Orient the scapula from the glenoid cavity and spine.
Relate the suprascapular nerve to the suprascapular notch.
Identify major muscular attachments of the coracoid process.
Relate scapular fossae to their muscles.
Identify the scapula in a rotatable upper-limb model.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Humeral landmarks and vulnerable structures
concepts.summary: The humerus links shoulder and elbow anatomy. Proximal tubercles and necks, the shaft's radial groove, and distal epicondyles and fossae predict muscle attachments, joint surfaces and characteristic nerve injuries.
keyPoints: The anatomical neck borders the head; the surgical neck lies distal to the tubercles and is related to the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.
The radial groove carries the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery on the posterior shaft.
The medial epicondyle is related posteriorly to the ulnar nerve; the lateral supracondylar region relates to the radial nerve.
Capitulum articulates with radius and trochlea with ulna; radial, coronoid and olecranon fossae accommodate movement.
examTraps: A surgical-neck injury threatens the axillary nerve, whereas a midshaft injury threatens the radial nerve.
The ulnar nerve is behind the medial epicondyle, not in the cubital fossa.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Match the three classic humeral injury levels to nerves.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Surgical neck—axillary; radial groove/midshaft—radial; medial epicondyle—ulnar.

objectives.text: Identify the humerus within the upper-limb skeleton.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints
concepts.summary: The sternoclavicular joint is the limb's only true bony articulation with the axial skeleton, while the acromioclavicular joint permits scapular adjustment. Discs and extracapsular ligaments distribute load across the girdle.
keyPoints: The sternoclavicular joint is synovial and contains an articular disc that separates joint surfaces and improves congruence.
Interclavicular and costoclavicular ligaments stabilize the medial clavicle.
The acromioclavicular joint is a small plane synovial joint; the coracoclavicular ligament is its major remote stabilizer.
Conoid and trapezoid parts of the coracoclavicular ligament resist vertical displacement after injury.
examTraps: Coracoclavicular is not the fibrous capsule of the acromioclavicular joint, yet it is its principal stabilizer.
Shoulder separation is an acromioclavicular/coracoclavicular injury, not glenohumeral dislocation.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can a coracoclavicular tear produce a prominent distal clavicle?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Loss of scapular suspension lets the limb and scapula drop relative to the clavicle.

objectives.text: Identify the coracoclavicular ligament as the principal vertical stabilizer of the acromioclavicular region.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Glenohumeral joint stability and relations
concepts.summary: The glenohumeral joint trades bony congruence for mobility. The labrum, capsule, glenohumeral ligaments, rotator cuff and coracoacromial arch provide complementary restraint while leaving an inferiorly vulnerable region.
keyPoints: The fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum deepens the shallow socket without eliminating mobility.
The long head of biceps tendon is intracapsular but extrasynovial and attaches near the supraglenoid region.
Rotator-cuff tendons blend with the capsule superiorly, anteriorly and posteriorly; inferior support is weakest.
The coracoacromial arch limits superior displacement; anterior-inferior dislocation can threaten the axillary nerve.
examTraps: Intracapsular does not mean within the synovial cavity for the long-head biceps tendon.
The labrum improves depth but is not the principal dynamic stabilizer.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is anteroinferior dislocation common?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The inferior capsule lacks a rotator-cuff reinforcement and is vulnerable when the abducted, externally rotated humeral head is forced anteriorly.

objectives.text: Explain how the glenoid labrum improves shoulder congruence.
Describe the intra-articular relation of the long biceps tendon.
Identify the glenohumeral joint and distinguish it from distal upper-limb joints.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Rotator-cuff muscles and functional stabilization
concepts.summary: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis form a musculotendinous cuff around the glenohumeral capsule. Their line of pull centers the humeral head while larger muscles generate movement.
keyPoints: Supraspinatus initiates abduction and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.
Infraspinatus and teres minor laterally rotate; subscapularis medially rotates.
Supraspinatus and infraspinatus receive suprascapular nerve supply; teres minor receives axillary supply.
Cuff tendons reinforce capsule except inferiorly; supraspinatus tendon is commonly impinged beneath the coracoacromial arch.
examTraps: Teres major is not a rotator-cuff muscle despite its name and proximity.
Deltoid is the major abductor after initiation, but does not center the head in the same cuff pattern.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: List the cuff in anterior-to-posterior order.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Subscapularis anteriorly, supraspinatus superiorly, then infraspinatus and teres minor posteriorly.

objectives.text: Match the suprascapular nerve to its two rotator-cuff muscles.
Integrate scapular topography with suprascapular-nerve supply.
Relate subscapularis to the posterior axillary wall.
Identify supraspinatus among the rotator-cuff muscles.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Quadrangular and triangular spaces
concepts.summary: Posterior scapular spaces are boundary-and-content problems. Teres minor, teres major, long-head triceps and humerus define routes that link axilla with the deltoid or scapular regions.
keyPoints: Quadrangular space: teres minor superior, teres major inferior, long-head triceps medial, surgical neck lateral.
Its contents are axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
Triangular space is bounded by teres minor, teres major and long-head triceps and transmits the circumflex scapular vessels.
The triangular interval transmits radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels toward the posterior arm.
examTraps: Do not exchange triangular space with triangular interval; their contents are different.
The axillary nerve does not traverse the triangular space.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What feature separates the quadrangular space from the triangular space?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The long head of triceps is the medial boundary of the quadrangular space and lateral boundary of the triangular space.

objectives.text: Assign the muscular boundaries of the quadrangular space.
Identify the contents of the quadrangular space.
Identify the axillary nerve in the quadrangular-space region.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Deltoid and axillary-nerve lesion logic
concepts.summary: The axillary nerve crosses the quadrangular space with posterior circumflex humeral vessels and winds around the surgical neck. Its motor and cutaneous territories make proximal humeral injury clinically recognizable.
keyPoints: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor.
Its superior lateral cutaneous branch supplies skin over the lower deltoid region.
Deltoid is the main abductor through the midrange after supraspinatus initiates movement.
Axillary injury causes deltoid wasting, flattened shoulder contour and a palpable humeral head.
examTraps: Loss of abduction after surgical-neck fracture is axillary, not suprascapular, when deltoid atrophy and badge-area sensory loss coexist.
Teres minor weakness affects lateral rotation but is less visually obvious than deltoid wasting.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What combined motor and sensory findings localize an axillary lesion?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Weak shoulder abduction with deltoid atrophy plus sensory loss over the superior lateral arm.

objectives.text: Localize axillary nerve injury at the surgical neck.
Identify the principal motor targets of the axillary nerve.
Recognize the visible consequence of axillary-nerve injury.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Posterior axillary gateways and scapular arterial route
concepts.summary: Quadrangular and triangular gateways connect the axilla with posterior scapular and deltoid regions, while suprascapular, dorsal scapular and circumflex scapular vessels form collateral channels around the scapula.
keyPoints: Quadrangular space transmits axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
Triangular space transmits circumflex scapular vessels from subscapular artery.
Suprascapular and dorsal scapular vessels connect subclavian-system supply to axillary-system circumflex scapular pathways.
The effectiveness of collateral flow depends on the level and completeness of axillary obstruction.
examTraps: Do not exchange triangular-space circumflex scapular vessels with quadrangular-space posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
An acute axillary injury remains clinically important even when a collateral network is present.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Contrast the two posterior-wall gateways.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Quadrangular space carries axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels; triangular space carries circumflex scapular vessels.

objectives.text: Distinguish triangular-space contents from adjacent gateways.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Lower-limb function, organization and key pathways
concepts.summary: The lower limb is organized for weight transfer, stance and locomotion. Bones, joints, fascial compartments, segmental innervation and superficial veins form the orientation framework for regional detail.
keyPoints: Body weight passes from axial skeleton through sacroiliac joints, pelvic ring, hip, femur, knee, tibia, ankle and foot arches.
Lumbar and sacral plexus branches distribute through anterior, medial and posterior pathways rather than mirroring upper-limb nerves.
Deep fascia creates thigh and leg compartments with characteristic action, nerve and arterial patterns.
Great and small saphenous veins are superficial routes connected to deep veins by perforators with valves.
examTraps: A lower-limb compartment label predicts a pattern but must be checked at transition zones and dual-action muscles.
Superficial veins do not simply duplicate named deep arteries.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the organizing mechanical task of the lower limb?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Transfer body weight while permitting stable stance and efficient locomotion.

objectives.text: Identify the tibia as the principal weight-bearing bone between the knee and ankle.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Hip bone, acetabulum and proximal femur
concepts.summary: Ilium, ischium and pubis fuse around the acetabulum, which receives the femoral head. Proximal-femoral angles and trochanters translate pelvic muscle force into gait and fracture patterns.
keyPoints: The acetabulum is formed by all three hip-bone components; its articular lunate surface surrounds a nonarticular fossa.
Femoral head faces medially, superiorly and slightly anteriorly; fovea anchors ligament of head.
Neck-shaft angle supports mobility and load transfer; decreased angle is coxa vara and increased angle coxa valga.
Greater and lesser trochanters are major muscle levers; linea aspera anchors thigh septa and muscles.
examTraps: The acetabular fossa is nonarticular, whereas the lunate surface is articular.
The ligament-of-head artery is more important in children than the retinacular supply in adults.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which bones contribute to the acetabulum?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Ilium, ischium and pubis.

objectives.text: Identify the components that form the acetabulum.
Distinguish coxa vara from coxa valga.
Identify the principal posterior landmark of the femoral shaft.
Identify the femur in a rotatable lower-limb model.
Identify the hip bone and distinguish it from lower-limb long bones.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Hip joint capsule, ligaments and stability
concepts.summary: The hip is a stable multiaxial synovial joint whose deep socket, labrum, capsule and spiral ligaments support weight bearing while permitting movement.
keyPoints: Acetabular labrum deepens the socket; transverse acetabular ligament bridges the notch.
Iliofemoral ligament strongly resists hyperextension; pubofemoral and ischiofemoral fibers reinforce other aspects.
Capsular fibers tighten in extension and loosen in flexion, explaining the close-packed extended position.
Retinacular vessels, chiefly from medial circumflex femoral artery, ascend along the neck beneath capsule.
examTraps: Ligament of head is not the main adult femoral-head blood supply.
Posterior dislocation threatens sciatic nerve even though the anterior iliofemoral ligament is strongest.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is standing stable with limited muscle effort?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Extension winds the spiral capsular ligaments tight, resisting further extension.

objectives.text: Explain avascular necrosis after an intracapsular femoral-neck fracture.
Relate the iliofemoral ligament to hip stability in standing.
Explain the close-packed stability of the extended hip.
Identify the nerve endangered by posterior hip dislocation.
Identify the source of the artery in the ligament of the femoral head.
Apply Hilton's law to hip-joint innervation.
Identify the hip joint and distinguish its major stabilizing ligament.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pelvic gateways to the lower limb
concepts.summary: The greater/lesser sciatic foramina, obturator canal and subinguinal space route nerves and vessels from pelvis into gluteal region, medial thigh and femoral triangle.
keyPoints: Piriformis divides greater sciatic foramen into supra- and infrapiriform routes.
Superior gluteal nerve/vessels pass above piriformis; sciatic and most other gluteal structures pass below.
Obturator nerve and vessels pass through obturator canal into medial thigh.
Femoral nerve, vessels and lymphatics pass beneath inguinal ligament in distinct muscular and vascular compartments.
examTraps: Piriformis exits the greater sciatic foramen; obturator internus tendon uses the lesser sciatic foramen.
Femoral nerve is outside femoral sheath even though it lies in the femoral triangle.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which structure divides the greater sciatic foramen into named routes?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Piriformis divides the greater sciatic foramen.

objectives.text: Use piriformis to organize structures at the greater sciatic foramen.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Gluteus maximus, medius, minimus and TFL
concepts.summary: Superficial gluteal muscles control hip extension and pelvic stability. Their differing insertions and superior/inferior gluteal innervation explain gait deficits.
keyPoints: Gluteus maximus extends the flexed hip and inserts largely into iliotibial tract; inferior gluteal nerve supplies it.
Gluteus medius and minimus abduct and stabilize the pelvis in single-leg stance; superior gluteal nerve supplies them.
Tensor fasciae latae also receives superior gluteal nerve and tensions iliotibial tract.
During stance, abductors on the supporting side prevent contralateral pelvic drop.
examTraps: A positive Trendelenburg sign reflects weakness on the stance side, while the pelvis drops on the unsupported side.
Gluteus maximus is less essential for level walking than rising, running or climbing.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Interpret a positive right Trendelenburg test.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Right hip abductors or their superior gluteal nerve are weak, so the left pelvis drops when standing on the right.

objectives.text: Recognize superior gluteal nerve injury from a Trendelenburg sign.
Relate gluteus maximus function to inferior gluteal innervation.
State the shared action of gluteus medius and minimus.
Identify gluteus medius and distinguish adjacent hip muscles.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Deep gluteal lateral rotators
concepts.summary: Piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli and quadratus femoris rotate the extended hip laterally and stabilize the femoral head; some abduct the flexed hip.
keyPoints: Piriformis passes through greater sciatic foramen to greater trochanter.
Obturator internus tendon bends through lesser sciatic foramen between gemelli.
Quadratus femoris runs from ischial tuberosity region to quadrate tubercle/intertrochanteric crest.
Short rotators lie near the sciatic nerve and serve as landmarks to gluteal neurovascular bundles.
examTraps: Obturator internus muscle arises in pelvis but its tendon enters gluteal region through lesser sciatic foramen.
Quadratus femoris is distinct from quadratus lumborum and femoral quadriceps.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which deep gluteal tendon passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Obturator internus tendon.

objectives.text: Identify quadratus femoris among the short lateral rotators.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Gluteal nerves, vessels and sciatic relations
concepts.summary: Piriformis is the reference for gluteal neurovascular exit. Superior gluteal structures pass above it; inferior gluteal, sciatic, posterior femoral cutaneous and other structures emerge below.
keyPoints: Superior gluteal nerve/vessels pass between gluteus medius and minimus.
Inferior gluteal nerve enters deep surface of gluteus maximus.
Sciatic nerve usually emerges below piriformis and descends deep to gluteus maximus midway between bony landmarks.
Inferior gluteal and internal pudendal systems have distinct courses despite both exiting below piriformis.
examTraps: Piriformis variations can split sciatic components, but standard questions usually use the usual undivided infrapiriform route.
Inferior gluteal artery is distinct from internal pudendal artery, which exits below piriformis and then enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which bundle uniquely exits superior to piriformis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Superior gluteal nerve and vessels.

objectives.text: Organize gluteal neurovascular structures around piriformis.
Distinguish superior and inferior gluteal vascular routes.
Explain the anatomic basis of piriformis syndrome.
Identify the sciatic nerve in the deep gluteal region.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Safe gluteal intramuscular injection
concepts.summary: Injection safety follows the map of sciatic nerve and major gluteal vessels. Superolateral or ventrogluteal sites reduce risk compared with inferomedial needle placement.
keyPoints: The sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal bundle occupy the deeper inferomedial gluteal region.
A superolateral quadrant avoids these major structures in the classic surface method.
The ventrogluteal site targets gluteus medius using iliac landmarks and also avoids sciatic nerve.
Needle depth and patient anatomy matter; the anatomical rule is risk reduction, not an absolute guarantee.
examTraps: Do not justify site choice solely by naming gluteus maximus; the key is avoiding neurovascular structures.
This anatomy source does not establish a current procedural protocol or dosing guidance.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the anatomical reason for a superolateral injection site?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It is remote from the sciatic nerve and major gluteal neurovascular bundles.

objectives.text: Choose a safe gluteal injection site from regional anatomy.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Femoral triangle, sheath and canal
concepts.summary: The femoral triangle is the proximal anterior-thigh gateway. Inguinal ligament, sartorius and adductor longus define it; lateral-to-medial nerve, artery, vein and canal relations organize examination and hernia logic.
keyPoints: Floor is iliopsoas laterally and pectineus/adductor longus medially; fascia lata forms roof.
From lateral to medial: femoral nerve, artery, vein, femoral canal/lymphatics.
Femoral sheath encloses artery, vein and canal but not femoral nerve.
Femoral canal permits venous expansion and contains lymphatics; a femoral hernia enters it medial to the vein.
examTraps: NAVEL is a relation mnemonic, not a statement that the nerve lies within the sheath.
A femoral hernia is below inguinal ligament and medial to femoral vein.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which femoral-triangle content is outside the femoral sheath?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath.

objectives.text: Order the femoral-triangle contents from lateral to medial.
Differentiate femoral-sheath contents from neighboring structures.
Localize the femoral canal and femoral hernia.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Anterior thigh muscles and femoral nerve
concepts.summary: Anterior thigh is a femoral-nerve compartment dominated by hip flexion and knee extension. Quadriceps arrangement and rectus femoris crossing two joints explain movement and patellar-reflex findings.
keyPoints: Quadriceps inserts through patella and patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity.
Rectus femoris crosses hip and knee; vasti cross only knee.
Sartorius flexes, abducts and laterally rotates hip while flexing knee.
Femoral nerve lesion weakens knee extension and reduces patellar reflex; saphenous nerve is its long sensory branch.
examTraps: Rectus femoris is not a hamstring despite crossing two joints.
Saphenous nerve is sensory and does not cause quadriceps weakness.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which quadriceps head flexes the hip as well as extending the knee?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Rectus femoris.

objectives.text: Localize femoral nerve injury from motor and reflex findings.
Distinguish rectus femoris from the vasti by joint crossings.
Identify the femoral nerve in the anterior thigh.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Medial thigh adductors and obturator nerve
concepts.summary: Adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis and obturator externus form a mostly obturator-nerve compartment. Adductor magnus bridges medial and posterior functional patterns.
keyPoints: Adductor longus and brevis adduct the hip and receive obturator nerve.
Gracilis crosses knee and inserts in pes anserinus, adding knee flexion/medial rotation.
Adductor magnus has adductor part supplied by obturator nerve and hamstring part supplied by tibial division of sciatic nerve.
Obturator externus laterally rotates and stabilizes the hip.
examTraps: Pectineus can receive femoral and/or obturator contribution; avoid treating it as a perfectly pure compartment marker.
Gracilis is the medial-thigh muscle that crosses the knee.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which adductor has dual functional and nerve-supply parts?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Adductor magnus.

objectives.text: Relate the obturator nerve to medial-thigh adduction.
Distinguish gracilis from the other medial-thigh muscles.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Hamstrings and sciatic divisions
concepts.summary: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris long head share ischial origin and tibial-division supply; short-head biceps is the key exception.
keyPoints: True hamstrings arise from ischial tuberosity, cross hip and knee, and receive tibial division of sciatic nerve.
They extend hip and flex knee; medial hamstrings medially rotate flexed leg, biceps laterally rotates.
Short head of biceps arises from femur, crosses only knee and receives common fibular division.
Sciatic nerve descends deep to hamstrings before dividing variably near popliteal fossa.
examTraps: Short-head biceps is not a true hamstring and is common-fibular supplied.
Hamstrings do not extend the knee; they flex it.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which posterior-thigh muscle is supplied by common fibular division?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Short head of biceps femoris.

objectives.text: Identify the innervation exception among the hamstrings.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Femoral/profunda arteries and adductor canal
concepts.summary: Femoral artery supplies the limb directly and through profunda femoris before traversing the adductor canal to become popliteal artery. Canal boundaries and exiting branches explain neurovascular transitions.
keyPoints: Profunda femoris gives medial/lateral circumflex femoral and perforating arteries.
Femoral artery enters adductor canal beneath sartorius with femoral vein, saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis.
The vessels leave via adductor hiatus and become popliteal; saphenous nerve pierces the canal roof before the hiatus.
Descending genicular artery also leaves the canal before the main femoral vessel exits.
examTraps: Both saphenous nerve and descending genicular artery leave before the hiatus; a stem asking simply 'which structure' is ambiguous.
Femoral nerve trunk is not a canal content, though saphenous and nerve to vastus medialis are branches.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which nerve accompanies vessels in the canal but does not pass through adductor hiatus?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Saphenous nerve.

objectives.text: Trace the femoral artery into the popliteal fossa.
Identify the principal deep artery of the thigh.
Trace the saphenous nerve through and out of the adductor canal.
Identify the femoral artery and distinguish its proximal and distal continuities.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Superficial veins and inguinal lymphatics
concepts.summary: Great saphenous vein ascends medially and pierces cribriform fascia to join femoral vein. Superficial and deep inguinal nodes receive distinct territories before drainage to external iliac nodes.
keyPoints: Great saphenous passes anterior to medial malleolus and enters femoral vein at saphenous opening.
Small saphenous passes posterior to lateral malleolus and usually enters popliteal vein.
Superficial inguinal nodes receive superficial lower limb and selected trunk/perineal territories.
Deep inguinal nodes lie medial to femoral vein; the highest deep node is in femoral canal region.
examTraps: Great saphenous is medial; small saphenous is posterior-lateral at ankle.
Superficial inguinal drainage exceptions should not be replaced by a blanket 'all superficial limb lymph'.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where does great saphenous vein join the deep system proximally?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It pierces cribriform fascia at the saphenous opening to enter femoral vein.

objectives.text: Trace the great saphenous vein to its deep venous termination.
Identify the great saphenous vein and its superficial course.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Knee articulations, capsule and bursae
concepts.summary: The knee combines tibiofemoral weight bearing with patellofemoral tracking. An incomplete fibrous capsule, synovial reflections and multiple bursae accommodate tendons and cruciate ligaments.
keyPoints: Femoral condyles articulate with tibial plateaus through menisci; patella articulates with trochlear surface.
Quadriceps tendon, patella and patellar ligament replace anterior fibrous capsule.
Cruciate ligaments are intracapsular but extrasynovial.
Suprapatellar bursa communicates with joint cavity; several other bursae may not.
examTraps: Intracapsular cruciates are outside the synovial cavity because synovium reflects around them.
Prepatellar bursitis is not identical to intra-articular effusion.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which knee ligaments are intracapsular but extrasynovial?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments.

objectives.text: Identify the knee joint in a rotatable lower-limb model.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Cruciate ligaments
concepts.summary: ACL and PCL cross within the intercondylar region to control anterior-posterior tibiofemoral translation and rotational stability.
keyPoints: ACL runs from anterior intercondylar tibia to posteromedial surface of lateral femoral condyle.
ACL resists anterior tibial translation and hyperextension.
PCL runs from posterior intercondylar tibia to lateral surface of medial femoral condyle.
PCL resists posterior tibial translation and is stronger than ACL.
examTraps: Name ligaments by tibial attachment and resisted tibial translation, not by which appears anterior in every view.
Drawer tests must specify whether tibia moves relative to femur.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which ligament restrains anterior translation of tibia?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

objectives.text: Interpret an anterior drawer test anatomically.
Recognize the mechanism of posterior cruciate ligament injury.
Trace the ACL from tibia to femur.
Identify the ACL among the principal stabilizing knee ligaments.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Menisci and collateral ligaments
concepts.summary: Menisci deepen tibial surfaces and distribute load; collateral attachments determine injury coupling. The medial meniscus is less mobile because it adheres to capsule and tibial collateral ligament.
keyPoints: Medial meniscus is C-shaped and attached to tibial collateral ligament.
Lateral meniscus is more circular and separated from fibular collateral ligament by popliteus tendon.
Tibial collateral ligament blends with medial capsule; fibular collateral is cordlike and extracapsular.
Meniscal horns attach in intercondylar area and move during flexion-extension.
examTraps: Fibular collateral ligament does not attach to lateral meniscus.
The popliteus tendon separates lateral meniscus from fibular collateral ligament.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is the medial meniscus more injury-prone?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Its firm capsular and tibial-collateral attachment makes it less mobile.

objectives.text: Explain the greater vulnerability of the medial meniscus.
Match valgus stress to the tibial collateral ligament.
Explain why the lateral meniscus is not tethered to the fibular collateral ligament.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Knee locking, unlocking and popliteus
concepts.summary: Terminal extension locks the knee through differential condylar motion; popliteus initiates flexion by reversing this rotation and also stabilizes posterolateral structures.
keyPoints: In weight bearing, femur medially rotates on fixed tibia during locking; in open chain, tibia laterally rotates on femur.
Popliteus unlocks by laterally rotating femur on fixed tibia or medially rotating free tibia.
Popliteus arises from lateral femoral condyle and inserts on posterior tibia above soleal line.
Locked extension tightens ligaments and permits stable standing with reduced muscular demand.
examTraps: Direction depends on whether femur or tibia is moving; state the fixed segment.
Popliteus does not powerfully flex the knee; it initiates unlocking.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does popliteus unlock a weight-bearing knee?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It laterally rotates the femur on the fixed tibia.

objectives.text: Explain the role of popliteus in knee unlocking.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Popliteal fossa boundaries and contents
concepts.summary: The diamond-shaped popliteal fossa is bounded by hamstrings and gastrocnemius. Its nerve-vein-artery depth order and vessel fixation explain examination and injury.
keyPoints: Superolateral boundary is biceps femoris; superomedial is semimembranosus/semitendinosus.
Inferior boundaries are medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius.
From superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery.
Common fibular nerve follows biceps tendon and winds around fibular neck.
examTraps: The popliteal artery is deepest, not easiest to palpate with the knee extended.
Common fibular nerve is a lateral boundary-related structure, not the central deepest content.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the central superficial-to-deep order?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery.

objectives.text: Order the major structures in the popliteal fossa by depth.
Localize common fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck.
Apply popliteal-fossa depth relationships during examination.
Identify the common fibular nerve at the lateral knee.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Tibia, fibula and tibiofibular joints
concepts.summary: Tibia bears weight and forms knee/ankle articulations; fibula provides lateral stability and muscle attachment. Interosseous membrane and tibiofibular joints coordinate force and ankle mortise integrity.
keyPoints: Tibial condyles receive femoral condyles; tibial tuberosity receives patellar ligament.
Fibular head articulates with lateral tibia but not femur and is related to common fibular nerve.
Distal tibiofibular syndesmosis stabilizes ankle mortise.
Interosseous membrane separates anterior and posterior planes and transmits forces between bones.
examTraps: Fibula contributes to ankle mortise but is not a weight-bearing participant at knee joint.
A high ankle sprain involves distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, not merely lateral ankle ligaments.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which bone carries most axial load through the leg?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The tibia is the principal weight-bearing leg bone.

objectives.text: Classify the distal tibiofibular joint as the syndesmosis stabilizing the ankle mortise.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Posterior leg compartments
concepts.summary: Posterior leg has superficial plantarflexors and deep flexor-invertor muscles, all supplied by tibial nerve. Popliteal artery divides into posterior and anterior tibial pathways at the proximal leg.
keyPoints: Gastrocnemius crosses knee and ankle; soleus crosses ankle only and is a postural plantarflexor.
Calcaneal tendon transmits triceps surae force; S1-S2 reflex tests tibial pathway.
Deep layer includes popliteus, FDL, tibialis posterior and FHL.
Posterior tibial artery descends with tibial nerve; fibular artery is its major branch.
examTraps: Soleus is unaffected by knee position, whereas gastrocnemius slackens with knee flexion.
Fibular artery usually arises from posterior tibial artery, not directly as the other terminal popliteal branch.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which muscle remains an effective plantarflexor with the knee flexed?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Soleus does not cross the knee joint.

objectives.text: Relate the calcaneal tendon reflex to its spinal levels.
Identify the usual origin of the fibular artery.
Assign motor innervation to the posterior leg.
Differentiate soleus from gastrocnemius by joint crossings.
Identify gastrocnemius and distinguish neighboring posterior structures.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Lateral leg compartment
concepts.summary: Fibularis longus and brevis evert the foot under superficial fibular-nerve supply. Their tendons pass behind lateral malleolus and diverge to distinct foot insertions.
keyPoints: Both muscles evert and weakly plantarflex.
Superficial fibular nerve supplies the compartment and becomes cutaneous distally.
Fibularis brevis inserts at base of fifth metatarsal.
Fibularis longus crosses sole to medial cuneiform/first metatarsal and supports transverse/longitudinal arches.
examTraps: Deep fibular nerve supplies anterior, not lateral, compartment.
An inversion injury may avulse fifth-metatarsal base through fibularis brevis traction.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which nerve supplies both fibularis longus and brevis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Superficial fibular nerve.

objectives.text: Recognize superficial fibular nerve injury.
State the primary action of the lateral leg compartment.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Anterior leg compartment
concepts.summary: Anterior leg dorsiflexors and toe extensors are supplied by deep fibular nerve and anterior tibial artery. Tight fascia makes this compartment vulnerable to pressure-related neurovascular dysfunction.
keyPoints: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes/inverts; EHL and EDL extend toes and dorsiflex; fibularis tertius assists eversion.
Deep fibular nerve supplies muscles and first-web-space skin distally.
Anterior tibial artery enters through proximal interosseous membrane and continues as dorsalis pedis.
Compartment syndrome impairs deep fibular function and dorsiflexion and threatens perfusion.
examTraps: Foot drop localizes to dorsiflexor weakness but can arise from common fibular, deep fibular or more proximal lesions; use sensory/eversion findings.
Dorsalis pedis is the continuation of anterior, not posterior, tibial artery.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What motor-sensory pair points to deep fibular dysfunction?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Weak dorsiflexion/toe extension with first-web-space sensory loss.

objectives.text: Relate deep fibular innervation to anterior-compartment function.
Trace the anterior tibial artery into the anterior compartment.
Localize neurologic loss in anterior-compartment syndrome.
Identify tibialis anterior and distinguish neighboring compartment muscles.
Identify the deep fibular nerve in the anterior leg.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Neurovascular transitions and superficial veins
concepts.summary: Named vessels and nerves change regions at specific apertures, while superficial veins cross predictable malleolar landmarks. These transitions integrate leg and foot localization.
keyPoints: Anterior tibial artery crosses proximal interosseous membrane; posterior tibial stays posterior and enters tarsal tunnel.
Common fibular divides into superficial and deep branches around fibular neck/proximal lateral compartment.
Great saphenous passes anterior to medial malleolus; small saphenous passes posterior to lateral malleolus.
Small saphenous usually ascends posterior calf to popliteal vein.
examTraps: Posterior tibial pulse is behind medial malleolus; dorsalis pedis is anterior on dorsum.
Common fibular lesion affects both dorsiflexion and eversion; isolated deep fibular lesion spares eversion.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which superficial vein is found posterior to the lateral malleolus?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Small saphenous vein.

objectives.text: Trace the small saphenous vein from ankle to popliteal fossa.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Foot bones, ankle and intertarsal joints
concepts.summary: Talus transmits tibial load to calcaneus and forefoot. The ankle primarily dorsiflexes/plantarflexes, whereas subtalar and transverse tarsal joints combine inversion/eversion.
keyPoints: Talocrural mortise is distal tibia/fibula around trochlea of talus.
Wider anterior talar trochlea makes dorsiflexion the more stable close-packed ankle position.
Subtalar and talocalcaneonavicular joints contribute coordinated inversion/eversion.
Medial deltoid ligament is strong; lateral complex includes anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular and posterior talofibular ligaments.
examTraps: Inversion sprain most often injures anterior talofibular ligament, not deltoid ligament.
Talus has no muscular attachments; its blood supply can be vulnerable in neck fractures/dislocation.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is ankle more stable in dorsiflexion?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The wider anterior trochlea of talus wedges into the mortise.

objectives.text: Relate the deltoid ligament to eversion stability.
Identify the typical ligament injured in a lateral ankle sprain.
Identify the ankle joint and distinguish it from the deltoid ligament.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Retinacula and tarsal tunnel
concepts.summary: Flexor retinaculum bridges medial ankle to form tarsal tunnel. Ordered tendons, vessels and tibial nerve pass posterior to medial malleolus before entering the sole.
keyPoints: From anterior to posterior: tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial vessels, tibial nerve, FHL.
Tibial nerve divides into medial and lateral plantar branches in or near the tunnel.
Posterior tibial pulse is palpated behind medial malleolus.
Compression can cause plantar pain/sensory disturbance and intrinsic weakness.
examTraps: FHL is the most posterior major tendon, not tibialis posterior.
Dorsalis pedis is not a tarsal-tunnel content.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Recite the tarsal-tunnel order anterior to posterior.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Tibialis posterior, FDL, vessels, tibial nerve, FHL.

objectives.text: Locate the posterior tibial artery at the ankle.
Identify the nerve at risk in tarsal tunnel syndrome.
Order the contents of the tarsal tunnel.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Medial, lateral and transverse arches
concepts.summary: The medial and lateral longitudinal arches and the transverse arch combine bone shape, ligaments, plantar aponeurosis and dynamic muscle support to distribute load during stance and walking.
keyPoints: The medial longitudinal arch is higher than the lateral longitudinal arch, which is lower and flatter against the ground.
The transverse arch is highest in the coronal plane through the head of the talus and disappears near the metatarsal heads.
Ligaments and the plantar aponeurosis provide passive support and help prevent separation of the ends of the arches.
Tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior and fibularis longus are named together as dynamic supports during walking.
examTraps: Do not reduce dynamic arch support to a two-tendon sling; Gray's names tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior and fibularis longus together.
The transverse arch has its maximum height through the talar head and flattens toward the metatarsal heads.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which three muscles are named together as dynamic arch supports?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior and fibularis longus.

objectives.text: Identify the muscular trio supporting the foot arches during walking.
Explain passive support of the longitudinal arch.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Plantar aponeurosis and fibrous toe sheaths
concepts.summary: The plantar aponeurosis is a thickening of deep fascia that protects deeper structures and supports the longitudinal arch; fibrous digital sheaths retain the long flexor tendons against the toes.
keyPoints: The central plantar aponeurosis is anchored to the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and divides into digital bands distally.
Plantar aponeurosis supports the longitudinal arch and protects deeper vessels, nerves and tendons.
Fibrous digital sheaths are attached along the margins of the phalanges and prevent the long flexor tendons from bowing during toe flexion.
Synovial sheaths surround the long flexor tendons within their fibrous tunnels to reduce friction.
examTraps: The plantar aponeurosis is not the same as long plantar ligament, though both support arches.
Heel pain may involve plantar-fascia origin, but anatomy alone does not define a treatment protocol.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where is the plantar aponeurosis anchored proximally?
retrievalPrompts.answer: To the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity.

objectives.text: Identify the proximal calcaneal attachment of the plantar aponeurosis.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Intrinsic muscles of the foot
concepts.summary: Dorsum contains short extensors; sole is organized in four layers around long tendons, plantar vessels and nerves. Interosseous actions use the second toe as the reference axis.
keyPoints: First layer: abductor hallucis, FDB, abductor digiti minimi.
Second layer includes quadratus plantae and lumbricals with FDL tendons.
Third layer includes FHB, adductor hallucis and flexor digiti minimi brevis.
Fourth layer contains dorsal/plantar interossei; dorsal abduct from second-toe axis, plantar adduct.
Long extensor tendons form dorsal digital expansions, with intrinsic foot muscles contributing to the extensor hoods of the toes.
examTraps: Second toe, not third, is the foot's abduction-adduction axis.
Quadratus plantae corrects the oblique pull of FDL rather than extending toes.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which toe is the reference axis for interosseous actions?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The second toe is the reference axis.

objectives.text: Apply the axial-digit rule to plantar interossei.
Distinguish dorsal from plantar interosseous actions.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Dorsalis pedis and plantar arterial arch
concepts.summary: Dorsalis pedis continues anterior tibial artery across dorsum; posterior tibial divides into plantar arteries, with lateral plantar forming most of the deep plantar arch.
keyPoints: Dorsalis pedis is palpated lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon on dorsum.
Deep plantar branch of dorsalis pedis joins lateral plantar artery.
Lateral plantar artery forms most of plantar arch and gives plantar metatarsal branches.
Medial plantar artery follows the medial sole and is generally smaller.
examTraps: Dorsalis pedis is a continuation of anterior tibial, not a branch of posterior tibial.
The plantar arch is mainly lateral plantar, unlike hand's mainly ulnar superficial arch.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which artery is the direct continuation of anterior tibial artery?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Dorsalis pedis.

objectives.text: Trace arterial continuity onto the dorsum of the foot.
Identify the posterior tibial artery along the posterior leg and ankle.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Plantar nerves and surface localization
concepts.summary: Medial and lateral plantar nerves distribute tibial motor and sensory supply through the sole. Surface landmarks integrate malleolar pulses, dorsalis pedis and tendon identification.
keyPoints: Medial plantar nerve supplies medial sole and medial three-and-a-half toes plus selected intrinsic muscles.
Lateral plantar nerve supplies lateral one-and-a-half toes and most intrinsic muscles through superficial/deep branches.
Deep branch of lateral plantar nerve accompanies plantar arch across the sole.
Posterior tibial pulse lies behind medial malleolus; dorsalis pedis is lateral to EHL tendon.
examTraps: Plantar digital territories resemble but do not exactly duplicate median/ulnar hand motor patterns.
First dorsal web-space sensation is deep fibular, not medial plantar.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which plantar nerve supplies most intrinsic foot muscles?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Lateral plantar nerve.

objectives.text: Identify the lateral plantar nerve as the motor supply to most intrinsic muscles of the sole.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Anterior arm compartment
concepts.summary: Biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis form the anterior arm compartment, supplied mainly by musculocutaneous nerve. Their attachments separate elbow flexion, supination and shoulder assistance.
keyPoints: Biceps inserts on radial tuberosity and via bicipital aponeurosis into forearm fascia; it flexes and powerfully supinates.
Brachialis inserts on ulna and is a dependable elbow flexor in any forearm position.
Coracobrachialis flexes/adducts the arm and is pierced by musculocutaneous nerve.
Musculocutaneous nerve continues as lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm after supplying the compartment.
examTraps: Biceps is a stronger supinator when the elbow is flexed; brachialis does not insert on radius.
Coracobrachialis is not a forearm muscle despite being pierced by a terminal nerve.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which attachment explains biceps supination?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Insertion on the radial tuberosity lets contraction rotate the radius into supination.

objectives.text: Relate musculocutaneous innervation to anterior-arm actions.
Relate biceps insertion to supination.
Identify biceps brachii and distinguish adjacent arm muscles.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Posterior arm compartment
concepts.summary: Triceps brachii and anconeus extend the elbow under radial-nerve supply. The radial nerve and profunda brachii travel together on the posterior humerus before the nerve returns anteriorly.
keyPoints: Long head of triceps crosses shoulder and elbow; lateral and medial heads arise from posterior humerus.
All heads converge on the olecranon; triceps is the chief elbow extensor.
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery occupy the radial groove between triceps attachments.
Anconeus assists extension and stabilizes the elbow while remaining radial-nerve supplied.
examTraps: The radial nerve can be injured at the shaft without necessarily paralyzing all triceps because proximal branches may already have arisen.
The long head helps define posterior scapular spaces in addition to extending the elbow.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What paired structures are endangered by a humeral shaft fracture at the radial groove?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery.

objectives.text: Identify radial innervation of the posterior arm.
Identify structures endangered in a humeral-shaft fracture.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Brachial artery and elbow collateral network
concepts.summary: The brachial artery continues the axillary artery, supplies the arm through profunda and collateral branches, and divides in the cubital fossa. Collateral/recurrent vessels preserve flow around the flexing elbow.
keyPoints: Brachial artery begins at inferior border of teres major and usually ends near radial neck as radial and ulnar arteries.
Profunda brachii accompanies radial nerve posteriorly.
Superior ulnar collateral accompanies ulnar nerve toward the posterior medial epicondyle.
Inferior ulnar collateral and radial/middle collateral branches join recurrent arteries around the elbow.
examTraps: The artery terminates in the cubital fossa near the radial neck, not at the elbow joint line by an absolute surface rule.
Profunda brachii is not the main continuation; it is a proximal deep branch.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which collateral artery follows the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Superior ulnar collateral artery.

objectives.text: Locate the normal brachial-artery bifurcation.
Relate elbow collateral vessels to nearby nerves.
Identify the brachial artery and distinguish its proximal and distal continuities.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Median, ulnar and radial nerve relations in arm
concepts.summary: Major nerves traverse the arm in characteristic relations even when they supply few or no arm muscles. These changing relations are a favorite localization framework.
keyPoints: Median nerve begins lateral to brachial artery and crosses anteriorly to lie medial in the distal arm.
Ulnar nerve pierces medial intermuscular septum and passes behind medial epicondyle.
Radial nerve passes posteriorly with profunda brachii, then pierces lateral intermuscular septum.
Musculocutaneous nerve lies within anterior compartment and becomes cutaneous near the elbow.
examTraps: Median nerve normally gives no major motor branch in arm despite its close arterial relation.
Ulnar nerve is not a content of the cubital fossa after passing behind the medial epicondyle.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which nerve changes from lateral to medial relative to the brachial artery?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The median nerve crosses the brachial artery.

objectives.text: Trace the ulnar nerve through the distal arm.
Trace the median nerve relative to the brachial artery.
Identify the radial nerve along the posterior arm.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Elbow and proximal radioulnar joints
concepts.summary: The elbow capsule encloses humeroulnar, humeroradial and proximal radioulnar articulations. Collateral ligaments guide hinge movement while the annular ligament retains the radial head during pronation-supination.
keyPoints: Trochlea with trochlear notch provides the principal hinge; capitulum meets radial head.
Ulnar collateral ligament resists valgus stress; radial collateral fibers blend with annular ligament.
Annular ligament encircles the radial head and attaches to ulna, allowing the head to rotate.
Flexion-extension occurs at elbow; pronation-supination requires proximal and distal radioulnar joints.
examTraps: The annular ligament attaches to ulna, not as a complete ring fixed to radius.
Pulled elbow is radial-head displacement from annular ligament in a child, not an ulnar collateral tear.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What structure retains the radial head while permitting rotation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The annular ligament.

objectives.text: Identify the annular ligament as the restraint that holds the radial head against the radial notch.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Cubital fossa boundaries, roof and contents
concepts.summary: The cubital fossa is a triangular anterior-elbow transition zone. Boundary and lateral-to-medial content order explain pulse palpation, venipuncture protection and nerve/vessel continuation.
keyPoints: Pronator teres forms medial boundary, brachioradialis lateral boundary, and epicondylar line the base.
Floor is brachialis and supinator; roof includes fascia strengthened by bicipital aponeurosis.
From lateral to medial: radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.
Brachial artery divides here; radial nerve divides into superficial and deep branches near the lateral fossa.
examTraps: The median cubital vein is in the superficial roof, not a deep content in the TAN order.
The ulnar nerve is posterior to the medial epicondyle, not inside the fossa.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: State the cubital-fossa order from lateral to medial.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.

objectives.text: Identify the boundaries and floor of the cubital fossa.
Order the principal contents of the cubital fossa.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Radius, ulna and radioulnar mechanics
concepts.summary: Radius and ulna form a stable proximal-distal pair linked by interosseous membrane. In pronation the radius crosses the ulna; in supination they are parallel.
keyPoints: Ulna dominates the elbow articulation; radius dominates the radiocarpal articulation.
Radial head rotates within annular ligament proximally; ulnar head articulates with radial ulnar notch distally.
Interosseous membrane transmits force and separates compartments while allowing coordinated rotation.
Pronation and supination rotate the radius around a longitudinal axis through radial head and distal ulna.
examTraps: Ulna does not directly articulate with carpal bones in the radiocarpal joint because an articular disc intervenes.
The radial tuberosity rotates posteriorly during pronation rather than remaining fixed anteriorly.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which forearm bone directly bears most carpal articulation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The radius rotates around the ulna.

objectives.text: Describe the radius rotating around the ulna during forearm pronation.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Superficial and intermediate anterior forearm muscles
concepts.summary: The superficial flexor-pronator group shares a medial epicondylar origin, while flexor digitorum superficialis forms an intermediate layer. Tendon insertion predicts which joints and phalanges each muscle moves.
keyPoints: Pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor carpi ulnaris arise wholly or partly from the common flexor origin.
Flexor digitorum superficialis splits to insert on middle phalanges of digits 2-5.
Flexor carpi radialis flexes and abducts wrist; flexor carpi ulnaris flexes and adducts.
Median nerve supplies the group except flexor carpi ulnaris, which is entirely ulnar supplied.
examTraps: Palmaris longus is variable and its absence does not imply median-nerve lesion.
FDS does not reach distal phalanges; FDP passes through its split.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why does FDS flex proximal interphalangeal joints?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Its split slips insert on the sides of middle phalanges.

objectives.text: Apply the median-nerve rule and its ulnar exceptions.
Identify the common flexor origin.
Distinguish FDS from FDP tendon insertions.
Identify pronator teres in the superficial anterior forearm.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Deep anterior forearm muscles
concepts.summary: Flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus and pronator quadratus form the deep anterior layer. Their split innervation and distal insertions make them valuable lesion-localization targets.
keyPoints: FDP inserts on distal phalanges of digits 2-5 and flexes distal interphalangeal joints.
Lateral FDP and flexor pollicis longus receive anterior interosseous branch of median nerve.
Medial FDP receives ulnar nerve.
Pronator quadratus is the deep distal pronator and is supplied by anterior interosseous nerve.
examTraps: An anterior interosseous lesion is motor; palmar cutaneous loss suggests a more proximal median lesion.
FDP is not wholly ulnar or wholly median supplied.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which muscles fail the OK-sign pinch after anterior interosseous injury?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Flexor pollicis longus and the lateral FDP component to the index finger.

objectives.text: Recognize anterior interosseous nerve palsy.
Use isolated joint testing to assess FDP.
Identify pronator quadratus from depth and innervation.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Anterior forearm arteries and nerves
concepts.summary: Radial and ulnar arteries and median/ulnar nerves traverse different fascial and tendinous planes. Surface relations at the wrist make these pathways clinically testable.
keyPoints: Radial artery follows lateral forearm and is palpated just lateral to flexor carpi radialis tendon.
Ulnar artery travels medially with ulnar nerve in the distal forearm; the nerve is usually medial to the artery.
Median nerve passes between FDS and FDP before entering carpal tunnel.
Anterior interosseous vessels and nerve descend on the interosseous membrane.
examTraps: The radial pulse landmark is lateral to FCR tendon, not lateral to brachioradialis tendon by default.
Ulnar artery and nerve enter the hand superficial to flexor retinaculum in Guyon canal, unlike median nerve.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which tendon is the key landmark for the radial pulse?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Flexor carpi radialis; the artery lies just lateral to it.

objectives.text: Locate the radial artery at the wrist.
Distinguish superficial and deep radial branches.
Identify the ulnar artery and distinguish the upper-limb arterial sequence.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Superficial posterior forearm muscles
concepts.summary: The superficial extensor-supinator group arises largely from the lateral epicondyle and is supplied by radial-nerve branches. Naming generally predicts action, but brachioradialis is the important flexor exception.
keyPoints: Brachioradialis flexes elbow most effectively in mid-pronation despite lying in the posterior/radial compartment.
ECRL and ECRB extend and abduct wrist; ECU extends and adducts.
Extensor digitorum expands into dorsal digital hoods; EDM and EI reinforce little/index extension.
Most superficial extensors share the common extensor origin at lateral epicondyle.
examTraps: Brachioradialis is radial supplied but flexes, so nerve does not alone predict action.
Finger extensors chiefly extend MCP joints directly; IP extension depends on the extensor expansion and intrinsic muscles.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which posterior-compartment muscle flexes the elbow?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Brachioradialis.

objectives.text: Recognize brachioradialis as the radial-nerve-supplied elbow flexor in the superficial posterior forearm group.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Deep posterior forearm muscles
concepts.summary: Supinator and the deep thumb/index extensors are supplied through the deep radial/posterior interosseous pathway. Their tendons create the snuffbox and specialized digit extension.
keyPoints: Deep radial nerve pierces supinator and continues as posterior interosseous nerve.
APL and EPB form the lateral snuffbox boundary; EPL forms the medial boundary.
EPL turns around Lister's tubercle before reaching the thumb.
Extensor indicis provides independent index extension and joins the extensor expansion.
examTraps: Posterior interosseous nerve is predominantly motor; dorsal hand sensory loss suggests superficial radial involvement instead.
EPL is in the third extensor compartment, not the first with APL and EPB.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which tendon forms the medial boundary of the anatomical snuffbox?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Extensor pollicis longus.

objectives.text: Trace the deep branch of the radial nerve into the posterior compartment.
Differentiate posterior interosseous motor loss from sensory nerve lesions.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Extensor retinaculum and six dorsal compartments
concepts.summary: The extensor retinaculum partitions dorsal wrist tendons into six synovial-lined compartments. Ordering the tendons from radial to ulnar explains snuffbox boundaries and tendon localization.
keyPoints: Compartment 1: APL and EPB; 2: ECRL and ECRB; 3: EPL.
Compartment 4: extensor digitorum and extensor indicis; 5: EDM; 6: ECU.
Lister's tubercle separates second and third compartments and redirects EPL.
Retinaculum prevents bowstringing and its septa create clinically distinct tendon tunnels.
examTraps: EPL is alone in compartment 3 and crosses obliquely; it is not grouped with EPB.
EDM occupies compartment 5, not compartment 4 with extensor digitorum.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Recite the six dorsal compartments from lateral to medial.
retrievalPrompts.answer: APL/EPB; ECRL/ECRB; EPL; ED/EI; EDM; ECU.

objectives.text: Map key tendons to dorsal extensor compartments.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Distal forearm surface relations
concepts.summary: Distal-forearm tendons and neurovascular structures create palpable lanes into the hand. These landmarks are useful only when radial-ulnar orientation and tendon actions are established first.
keyPoints: Radial artery is lateral to FCR tendon; median nerve lies deep between FCR and palmaris-longus region before carpal tunnel.
Ulnar artery and nerve lie lateral to FCU tendon and pass superficial to flexor retinaculum.
Palmaris longus, when present, tenses palmar aponeurosis and is superficial to retinaculum.
Dorsal tendons can be identified by resisted thumb/finger movements and their six compartments.
examTraps: Median nerve is not consistently identifiable as a superficial tendon.
The ulnar neurovascular bundle is lateral—not medial—to FCU tendon at the wrist.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where is the radial pulse relative to FCR?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Immediately lateral to the FCR tendon.

objectives.text: Use palmaris longus as a surface landmark for the median nerve.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Anatomical snuffbox
concepts.summary: Thumb extension exposes a triangular dorsolateral depression bounded by APL/EPB laterally and EPL medially. The radial artery crosses its floor over scaphoid and trapezium.
keyPoints: Lateral boundary is APL and EPB; medial boundary is EPL.
Floor includes scaphoid and trapezium with ECRL/ECRB tendons deeper in the region.
Radial artery passes through the snuffbox before entering the palm.
Scaphoid tenderness after a fall is clinically important even when early radiographs are unrevealing.
examTraps: Superficial radial nerve and cephalic vein cross the roof; they are not the deep arterial content.
EPL is medial, while EPB is lateral.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What are the boundary tendons and principal deep content?
retrievalPrompts.answer: APL/EPB laterally, EPL medially, and radial artery crossing the floor.

objectives.text: Identify the vascular content of the anatomical snuffbox.
Identify the tendon boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Carrying angle and upper-limb alignment
concepts.summary: The carrying angle is the lateral deviation between arm and forearm axes in extension and supination. It positions the hand away from the hip during carrying and changes with elbow position.
keyPoints: The angle is assessed with elbow extended and forearm supinated.
It disappears or diminishes with flexion and pronation.
Its direction is valgus: forearm deviates laterally relative to arm.
Marked changes can follow distal humeral malalignment and alter ulnar-nerve mechanics.
examTraps: Do not describe the normal carrying angle as medial deviation.
A measured angle without standardized elbow/forearm position is not comparable.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: In which direction does the forearm deviate in the normal carrying angle?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The forearm deviates laterally in anatomical position.

objectives.text: Describe the direction and functional significance of the carrying angle.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Radiocarpal and midcarpal movement
concepts.summary: Wrist movement is distributed across radiocarpal and midcarpal articulations. Radius and articular disc meet the proximal carpal row, while muscular pairs combine flexion-extension with radial-ulnar deviation.
keyPoints: Scaphoid and lunate articulate with the distal radius; the triquetrum articulates with the articular disc on the ulnar side of the wrist joint.
Ulna is excluded from direct carpal articulation by the triangular fibrocartilage complex.
Flexion-extension occurs across radiocarpal and midcarpal joints; radial/ulnar deviation uses coordinated carpal motion.
Balanced wrist extension stabilizes the hand for powerful finger flexion.
examTraps: The ulna does not directly form the radiocarpal articular surface.
A muscle's wrist action depends on its tendon position relative to both flexion-extension and deviation axes.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which forearm bone directly articulates with the proximal carpal row?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The radius, with an articular disc occupying the ulnar side.

objectives.text: Identify the radius as the forearm bone directly articulating with the scaphoid and lunate.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Carpal, metacarpal and phalangeal joints
concepts.summary: Eight carpal bones form proximal and distal rows that distribute load and create the carpal arch. Thumb carpometacarpal geometry permits opposition, while MCP and interphalangeal joints separate gross and precision movement.
keyPoints: Proximal row lateral-to-medial is scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal row is trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
