Flexor retinaculum bridges carpal concavity to form carpal tunnel.
First carpometacarpal joint is saddle-shaped and permits opposition through combined abduction, flexion and rotation.
MCP joints allow flexion-extension and abduction-adduction; IP joints are hinge joints.
examTraps: Pisiform is a sesamoid in FCU tendon and does not share the same radiocarpal role as scaphoid/lunate.
Opposition is not simple flexion; medial rotation of the first metacarpal is essential.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Name the carpal bones by row from lateral to medial.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.

objectives.text: Recognize the vascular complication of scaphoid fracture.
Identify the carpal bones and distinguish adjacent hand skeleton groups.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Carpal tunnel and flexor retinaculum
concepts.summary: The flexor retinaculum roofs a rigid osteofibrous tunnel containing median nerve and nine long-flexor tendons. Neighboring tendons and the ulnar canal are separate and are frequent distractors.
keyPoints: Tunnel contents: median nerve, four FDS, four FDP and one FPL tendon.
FCR tendon occupies its own compartment in the retinacular region rather than the main tunnel.
Ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to retinaculum in Guyon canal.
Median compression impairs thenar recurrent motor function and lateral digital sensation, while palmar cutaneous sensation may be spared.
examTraps: FCR is not one of the nine main carpal-tunnel tendons.
Thenar weakness from carpal tunnel does not imply ulnar-canal compression.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which tendon lies in a separate retinacular compartment?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Flexor carpi radialis.

objectives.text: Enumerate the contents and exclusions of the carpal tunnel.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Palmar aponeurosis and digital fibrous sheaths
concepts.summary: Palmar fascia anchors skin for grip, while fibrous digital sheaths retain flexor tendons against phalanges. Synovial sheaths reduce friction but create clinically relevant routes for infection.
keyPoints: Palmar aponeurosis is a triangular condensation of deep fascia, continuous proximally with palmaris longus when present and the flexor retinaculum.
Fibrous digital sheaths form pulley tunnels attached to the phalanges and palmar plates and prevent flexor-tendon bowstringing.
Within the carpal tunnel all FDS and FDP tendons share one synovial sheath, while FPL has a separate sheath; the thumb and little-finger digital sheaths commonly continue proximally.
Vessels, nerves and long flexor tendons lie deep to the palmar aponeurosis, while palmaris brevis lies in superficial fascia over the hypothenar region.
examTraps: Palmar aponeurosis is a condensation of deep fascia and lies superficial to, but does not form, the flexor retinaculum or carpal-tunnel roof.
Digital sheath continuity differs by digit; do not assume every infection communicates identically with the wrist.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why do fibrous digital sheaths matter mechanically?
retrievalPrompts.answer: They prevent flexor tendons from bowstringing away from phalanges during flexion.

objectives.text: Explain how a fibrous digital sheath prevents flexor-tendon bowstringing.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Extensor hoods and intrinsic-extensor integration
concepts.summary: The extensor expansion distributes extrinsic and intrinsic tendon force across MCP and IP joints. This explains why lumbricals and interossei can flex MCP joints while extending IP joints.
keyPoints: The extensor hood apex attaches to the distal phalanx, while its central region attaches to the middle phalanx.
Interossei insert into both proximal phalanges and extensor hoods; lumbricals attach to the extensor hoods without a proximal-phalanx insertion.
Intrinsic muscles pass palmar to MCP axes but dorsal to IP axes through the hood.
Retinacular structures coordinate lateral-band position through flexion and extension.
examTraps: Extensor digitorum alone does not fully explain coordinated IP extension.
Interossei are not pure abductors/adductors; their hood insertion enables IP extension.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How can an interosseous muscle flex MCP yet extend IP joints?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Its proximal course is palmar to the MCP axis while its extensor-expansion insertion acts dorsally at IP joints.

objectives.text: Identify the distal-phalanx attachment of the extensor hood apex.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Thenar, hypothenar, lumbrical and interosseous muscles
concepts.summary: Intrinsic hand muscles position the thumb and digits for precision. Median nerve dominates thenar opposition and lateral lumbricals; deep ulnar branch supplies most other intrinsic muscles.
keyPoints: Thenar muscles abduct, flex and oppose the thumb; recurrent median nerve is the major motor branch.
Adductor pollicis is supplied by deep ulnar branch and is tested by key pinch.
Dorsal interossei abduct digits from the third-digit axis; palmar interossei adduct toward it.
Lumbricals flex MCP and extend IP joints; lateral two are median supplied and medial two ulnar supplied.
examTraps: The third digit is the reference axis: it can abduct in either direction and has no palmar interosseous.
Adductor pollicis is not recurrent-median supplied despite being in the thumb region.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What mnemonic distinguishes interosseous actions?
retrievalPrompts.answer: DAB for dorsal abduct; PAD for palmar adduct, around the third-digit axis.

objectives.text: Apply the palmar-adduct/dorsal-abduct rule.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Superficial and deep palmar arches
concepts.summary: Radial and ulnar arteries form communicating arches that distribute blood to palm and digits. The ulnar artery predominates superficially; radial artery predominates deeply.
keyPoints: Superficial palmar arch is mainly ulnar and gives common palmar digital arteries.
Deep palmar arch is mainly radial and lies deeper across metacarpal bases.
Radial artery enters palm after crossing snuffbox and passing between heads of first dorsal interosseous.
Princeps pollicis and radialis indicis usually arise from radial-side circulation.
examTraps: Both arches are anastomotic; 'mainly' does not mean exclusively one artery.
The superficial arch is distal to the deep arch and closer to palmar aponeurosis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which artery is the principal contributor to each arch?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Ulnar to superficial arch; radial to deep arch.

objectives.text: Distinguish arterial contributions to the palmar arches.
Identify the principal source of the deep palmar arch.
Identify the superficial palmar arch in the interactive hand model.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Median and ulnar nerves in hand
concepts.summary: Median and ulnar nerves divide into motor and digital branches after crossing different wrist tunnels. Sensory territories and intrinsic-muscle patterns distinguish carpal-tunnel, Guyon-canal and proximal lesions.
keyPoints: Median nerve enters carpal tunnel and gives recurrent thenar and common/proper digital branches.
Ulnar nerve enters Guyon canal superficial to flexor retinaculum and divides into superficial sensory and deep motor branches.
Median supplies lateral three-and-a-half palmar digits; ulnar supplies medial one-and-a-half in the standard pattern.
Deep ulnar branch supplies interossei, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis and medial lumbricals.
examTraps: Thenar skin can be spared in carpal-tunnel syndrome because palmar cutaneous median branch arises proximally and passes superficial to retinaculum.
Guyon-canal lesions can spare dorsal ulnar hand sensation because dorsal cutaneous branch arises in forearm.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How can sensory sparing distinguish carpal-tunnel from a proximal median lesion?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Thenar-eminent skin is often spared in carpal tunnel but may be involved in a proximal lesion.

objectives.text: Localize ulnar-nerve compression at the wrist.
Relate recurrent median innervation to thumb opposition.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Axillary inlet, walls and floor
concepts.summary: The axilla is a pyramidal passage between neck, thoracic wall and upper limb. Its apex, four walls and skin/fascial floor provide a stable map for locating vessels, nerves and lymph nodes.
keyPoints: The apex is bounded by clavicle, first rib and superior border of scapula.
Anterior wall is pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, subclavius and clavipectoral fascia.
Medial wall is thoracic wall with serratus anterior; posterior wall is subscapularis above and teres major/latissimus dorsi below.
The narrow lateral wall is the intertubercular region of humerus; the floor is skin, superficial fascia and axillary fascia.
examTraps: Serratus anterior forms the medial wall, not the posterior wall.
Coracobrachialis is a content beside the lateral wall rather than a primary wall-forming muscle.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Reconstruct the axilla from its apex and four walls.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Apex: clavicle/first rib/scapula; anterior: pectoral muscles and fascia; medial: ribs/serratus; posterior: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus; lateral: proximal humerus.

objectives.text: Define the cervicoaxillary canal.
Locate subclavius in the anterior axillary wall.
Differentiate posterior and medial axillary walls.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Clavipectoral fascia and axillary floor
concepts.summary: Clavipectoral fascia encloses subclavius and pectoralis minor and continues inferiorly as the suspensory ligament of the axilla. Structures piercing it link superficial deltopectoral tissues with deeper axillary contents.
keyPoints: The fascia extends from clavicle to axillary fascia and invests subclavius and pectoralis minor.
The thick costocoracoid membrane lies between subclavius and pectoralis minor.
Cephalic vein pierces the fascia to join the axillary vein.
Thoracoacromial vessels and lateral pectoral nerve also cross this fascial plane.
examTraps: The cephalic vein is superficial in the deltopectoral groove before piercing clavipectoral fascia.
The suspensory ligament is a continuation of clavipectoral fascia, not the pectoralis major tendon.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Name the clinically recognizable vein that pierces clavipectoral fascia.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The cephalic vein.

objectives.text: Identify structures piercing the clavipectoral fascia.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Axillary artery parts and branches
concepts.summary: Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts, creating a branch-counting framework and a central reference for cords of the brachial plexus.
keyPoints: The artery begins at the lateral border of the first rib and becomes brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major.
First part usually gives superior thoracic artery; second gives thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries.
Third part gives subscapular and anterior/posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
Cords of the brachial plexus are named by relation to the second part of the artery.
examTraps: The part number follows relation to pectoralis minor, not chronological order of named branches.
Subscapular is a third-part branch, whereas circumflex scapular is a branch of subscapular.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How can the branches be recalled by part?
retrievalPrompts.answer: One branch from first part, two from second, and three from third, using the usual pattern.

objectives.text: Define the parts of the axillary artery using pectoralis minor.
Match major axillary branches to their parts.
Identify the axillary artery and distinguish its continuities.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Axillary vein and superficial venous connections
concepts.summary: The axillary vein lies anteromedial to the artery and receives tributaries corresponding broadly to arterial branches plus the cephalic vein. Its thin wall and changing relation matter in access and injury.
keyPoints: It forms near the inferior border of teres major from basilic vein and paired brachial veins.
It becomes subclavian vein at the lateral border of the first rib.
The cephalic vein enters after traversing the deltopectoral groove and clavipectoral fascia.
The vein is generally medial/anterior to the artery and is not enclosed by brachial-plexus cords in the same way.
examTraps: Do not apply the artery's pectoralis-minor three-part naming scheme to the axillary vein.
Cephalic is lateral and superficial; basilic is medial and contributes to formation of axillary vein.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where does the axillary vein become the subclavian vein?
retrievalPrompts.answer: At the lateral border of the first rib.

objectives.text: Locate the axillary-to-subclavian venous transition at the lateral border of the first rib.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Axillary lymph-node groups and drainage
concepts.summary: Axillary lymph nodes are organized around vessels and walls, then converge through central to apical groups. Their drainage territories connect upper limb, thoracic wall and breast anatomy.
keyPoints: Humeral/lateral nodes receive most upper-limb lymph except channels accompanying cephalic vein.
Pectoral/anterior nodes receive anterior thoracic wall and much of the breast.
Subscapular/posterior nodes receive posterior thoracic wall and scapular region.
Central nodes receive the preceding groups; apical nodes receive central and cephalic-associated pathways before forming the subclavian lymph trunk.
examTraps: Cephalic-associated lymph can bypass humeral nodes toward deltopectoral/apical nodes.
Node groups are named for relations, not necessarily the diseases that reach them.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which axillary group is the final common intraxillary recipient before the subclavian trunk?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Apical nodes receive the converging axillary drainage.

objectives.text: Identify the humeral axillary nodes as the recipients of most upper-limb lymph.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Brachial plexus roots, trunks, divisions and cords
concepts.summary: The brachial plexus reorganizes C5-T1 ventral rami through roots, trunks, anterior/posterior divisions and cords before terminal branches. Relations to scalene muscles, clavicle and axillary artery provide the three-dimensional map.
keyPoints: C5-C6 form upper trunk, C7 continues as middle trunk, and C8-T1 form lower trunk.
Each trunk splits into anterior and posterior divisions behind the clavicle.
Anterior divisions generally supply flexor compartments; posterior divisions unite as posterior cord and generally supply extensors.
Cords are lateral, medial and posterior relative to the second part of the axillary artery.
examTraps: Cord names are not relations to the body midline.
The upper trunk is C5-C6; adding C7 describes the lateral cord contribution, not the upper trunk.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace C5 from root to a terminal branch.
retrievalPrompts.answer: C5 contributes to upper trunk, its divisions, and ultimately multiple cords/branches including musculocutaneous, axillary and suprascapular pathways.

objectives.text: Construct the root-to-trunk organization of the brachial plexus.
Explain how the brachial-plexus cords are named.
Identify the upper trunk within the brachial plexus overlay.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Branches from roots and upper trunk
concepts.summary: Proximal plexus branches reveal lesion level. Dorsal scapular and long thoracic arise from roots, while suprascapular and nerve to subclavius arise from the upper trunk.
keyPoints: Dorsal scapular nerve usually arises from C5 and supplies rhomboids and levator scapulae.
Long thoracic nerve receives C5-C7 contributions and descends on serratus anterior.
Suprascapular nerve comes from upper trunk and supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
Nerve to subclavius also arises from upper trunk and may communicate with phrenic nerve.
examTraps: Long thoracic injury causes winging because serratus anterior cannot hold the medial border to the thoracic wall.
Suprascapular is a trunk branch, not a posterior-cord branch.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which proximal branch is tested by asking a patient to push against a wall?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Long thoracic nerve through serratus anterior function.

objectives.text: Recognize long thoracic nerve injury from scapular winging.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Lateral cord branches
concepts.summary: The lateral cord derives from anterior divisions of upper and middle trunks and produces lateral pectoral, musculocutaneous and lateral root of median nerve.
keyPoints: Lateral pectoral nerve crosses toward pectoral muscles and may communicate with medial pectoral nerve.
Musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, supplies anterior arm and continues as lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm.
The lateral root joins the medial root to form median nerve.
Its C5-C7 bias explains overlap with upper/middle-trunk functions.
examTraps: Median nerve is formed by two roots; neither lateral nor medial cord alone is the complete nerve.
Lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm is the continuation of musculocutaneous nerve, not a radial branch.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Name the three principal lateral-cord branches.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Lateral pectoral, musculocutaneous and lateral root of median nerve.

objectives.text: Map terminal branches to brachial-plexus cords.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Medial cord branches
concepts.summary: The medial cord continues the anterior division of the lower trunk and contributes pectoral, cutaneous and major terminal branches with a C8-T1 emphasis.
keyPoints: Branches include medial pectoral, medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm, ulnar nerve and medial root of median nerve.
Ulnar nerve is the major terminal continuation and is strongly C8-T1 weighted.
The medial root crosses to unite with the lateral root around the axillary artery.
Medial cutaneous nerves supply skin and communicate with neighboring cutaneous territories.
examTraps: Medial cord is named relative to axillary artery, not because every branch supplies anatomically medial muscles.
Ulnar nerve is not formed by both lateral and medial roots; that pattern belongs to median nerve.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which terminal nerve is the major continuation of the medial cord?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The ulnar nerve.

objectives.text: Identify the medial-cord terminal branch.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Posterior cord branches
concepts.summary: All three posterior divisions unite as posterior cord. Its subscapular and thoracodorsal branches serve posterior-wall muscles, while axillary and radial nerves supply major extensor-region targets.
keyPoints: Upper subscapular supplies subscapularis; lower subscapular supplies subscapularis and teres major.
Thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi.
Axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor and crosses the quadrangular space.
Radial nerve is the large terminal branch supplying posterior arm/forearm compartments and posterior limb skin.
examTraps: Teres major receives lower subscapular nerve, whereas teres minor receives axillary nerve.
Thoracodorsal nerve is a posterior-cord branch despite its course on the posterior axillary wall.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which posterior-cord branches accompany the posterior wall versus the quadrangular space?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Subscapular/thoracodorsal branches follow the posterior wall; axillary nerve enters the quadrangular space.

objectives.text: Identify the terminal branches of the posterior cord.
Identify the posterior cord around the axillary artery.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Upper- and lower-plexus lesion patterns
concepts.summary: Plexus lesion questions are solved by level and lost muscle groups, not by memorized posture alone. Upper-trunk lesions remove C5-C6-dominant shoulder/elbow functions; lower-trunk lesions emphasize C8-T1 intrinsic-hand weakness.
keyPoints: Upper-trunk injury weakens abduction, lateral rotation, elbow flexion and supination, producing the classic adducted, medially rotated, extended and pronated posture.
Lower-trunk injury weakens intrinsic hand muscles and may produce clawing.
Long-thoracic injury is a proximal branch lesion with scapular winging rather than a full trunk syndrome.
Terminal nerve deficits should be distinguished from multi-nerve trunk patterns.
examTraps: A posture label is not enough: verify the affected roots and multiple nerve territories.
Clawing from lower-plexus injury is broader than an isolated distal ulnar lesion when median C8-T1 fibers are also involved.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What functional cluster points to an upper-trunk lesion?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Loss of shoulder abduction/lateral rotation plus weak elbow flexion and supination across axillary, suprascapular and musculocutaneous territories.

objectives.text: Recognize an upper-trunk brachial-plexus palsy.
Recognize a lower-trunk brachial-plexus palsy.

concepts.subject: embryology
concepts.title: Limb growth, axes, joints, and muscle patterning
concepts.summary: Limb buds contain somatic-lateral-plate mesenchyme for bone and connective tissue plus migrating somite-derived myoblasts. AER FGFs maintain distal proliferation while flank retinoic acid supports proximal differentiation. SHH from the posterior ZPA patterns the anteroposterior axis, and EN1-WNT7a-LMX1 establishes dorsoventral identity. Opposite limb rotations create adult compartment orientation. Joint interzones and programmed cell death shape articulations and digits.
keyPoints: AER loss truncates the limb according to timing because differentiation proceeds proximodistally.
Interdigital apoptosis separates rays after the AER has subdivided into digit-specific segments.
WNT14 is presented as a likely joint-interzone inducer, but exact joint-position regulation remains incomplete.
Lateral-plate connective tissue patterns somite-derived muscle masses.
TBX5 specifies forelimb; TBX4 with PITX1 specifies hindlimb; WNT7a helps maintain SHH as well as dorsal identity.
examTraps: This entire concept is book extension and is not confirmed by the provided Term 2 limb lectures or past exams.
Do not confuse muscle-cell origin with connective-tissue control of muscle pattern.
Upper and lower limbs rotate in opposite directions.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What happens after early AER loss?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Already specified proximal structures may remain, while later distal zeugopod and autopod structures are truncated.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does ectopic anterior SHH cause?
retrievalPrompts.answer: A second polarizing center and mirror-image digit duplication.

objectives.text: Apply tissue lineages, growth-zone signaling, rotations, joint morphogenesis, and axial patterning to limb-development scenarios.

concepts.title: Axilla, arm and cubital fossa pathways
concepts.summary: Axillary and arm anatomy is a set of predictable relationships around named vessels and fascial transitions. Cord-derived branch positions, scapular collateral flow, nodal sequence and radial-nerve compartment changes can all be derived from this spatial framework.
keyPoints: Axillary and radial nerves, both posterior-cord branches, lie posterior to the third part of the axillary artery.
The suprascapular and circumflex scapular systems connect subclavian inflow with distal axillary flow around a proximal block.
Most upper-limb lymph passes humeral to central to apical axillary nodes.
The radial nerve travels in the radial groove, gives cutaneous branches there, then pierces the lateral intermuscular septum.
In the cubital fossa the radial nerve divides into superficial and deep branches; the bicipital aponeurosis protects deeper artery and median nerve during venepuncture.
examTraps: A branch's cord of origin predicts its relation to the axillary artery only after identifying which part of the artery is being described.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace the radial nerve from posterior arm to its terminal division.
retrievalPrompts.answer: It accompanies profunda brachii in the radial groove, pierces the lateral intermuscular septum, reaches the lateral cubital fossa and divides into superficial and deep branches.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which scapular connection can carry blood past a proximal axillary obstruction?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Subclavian branches such as suprascapular connect with circumflex scapular, which communicates with the subscapular/third-part axillary system.

concepts.title: Wrist and hand mechanics and lesions
concepts.summary: Hand questions become discriminating when tendon paths and joint axes are tied to lesion level. The extensor expansion integrates intrinsic muscles, dorsal compartments localize tendons, and preserved long flexors determine the appearance of ulnar and median neuropathies.
keyPoints: Lumbricals pass anterior to metacarpophalangeal axes but insert into dorsal expansions, producing MCP flexion with IP extension.
The fourth dorsal compartment contains extensor digitorum and extensor indicis; neighboring thumb and little-finger tendons occupy different compartments.
The radial artery lies on the floor of the anatomical snuffbox while the cephalic vein and superficial radial nerve cross superficially.
The median palmar cutaneous branch passes outside the carpal tunnel, explaining relative central-palm sensory sparing.
Froment sign uses flexor pollicis longus to compensate for adductor pollicis weakness.
A distal ulnar lesion can claw more because ulnar flexor digitorum profundus remains active; a proximal lesion weakens that flexor and reduces the claw.
examTraps: Do not equate a more proximal lesion with a more dramatic posture; the visible deformity depends on which antagonists are also denervated.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why do lumbricals flex MCP joints but extend IP joints?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Their line of pull is palmar to the MCP axis but joins the dorsal extensor expansion beyond it.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is palmar skin often spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The median palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to and travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

concepts.title: Femoral, gluteal and thigh relationships
concepts.summary: The proximal lower limb is organized by gates and tunnels. Femoral-ring boundaries predict hernia hazards, sciatic foramina route structures between regions, and the adductor canal connects the femoral triangle to the popliteal fossa while preserving a distinctive nerve-muscle pattern.
keyPoints: The femoral ring is bounded by inguinal ligament anteriorly, lacunar ligament medially, femoral vein laterally and pectineal structures posteriorly.
The femoral canal is a potential space that permits femoral-vein expansion.
The lesser sciatic foramen transmits obturator internus tendon, pudendal neurovascular structures and the nerve to obturator internus.
Medial circumflex femoral retinacular branches dominate adult femoral-head blood supply and participate in the trochanteric anastomosis.
The adductor canal is between vastus medialis and adductors, roofed by subsartorial fascia.
examTraps: Femoral nerve is lateral to and outside the femoral sheath; it is not a femoral-canal content.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: List the femoral-ring boundaries clockwise from anterior.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Inguinal ligament anterior, femoral vein lateral, pectineal ligament/pectineus posterior, lacunar ligament medial.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What roofs the adductor canal, and which muscle overlies that roof?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Subsartorial fascia forms its anteromedial roof, overlain by sartorius; vastus medialis and the adductors form its muscular walls.

concepts.title: Popliteal, ankle and foot integration
concepts.summary: At the posterolateral knee and through the sole, tendon paths are more reliable than isolated labels. The popliteus-meniscus relationship and oblique plantar supports predict both surgical risk and patterns of arch failure.
keyPoints: The popliteus tendon is intracapsular and extrasynovial, deep to the fibular collateral ligament and related to the lateral meniscus.
Fibularis longus crosses the sole through a cuboid tunnel to the first metatarsal base and medial cuneiform, contributing to transverse-arch support.
The long plantar ligament and the plantar cuboid groove together complete the osseofibrous tunnel that redirects fibularis longus across the sole.
The spring ligament forms a fibrocartilaginous support under the talar head and is central to medial longitudinal arch stability.
examTraps: Intracapsular does not necessarily mean within the synovial cavity; popliteus and cruciate structures are key examples.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is the popliteus tendon described as intracapsular but extrasynovial?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It lies within the fibrous capsule but is invested by synovium on its deep surface, outside the synovial cavity; it also grooves the lateral meniscus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which two new items distinguish transverse and medial-longitudinal arch support?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Fibularis longus crosses the sole toward the first ray and supports the transverse arch; the spring ligament directly cradles the talar head in the medial longitudinal arch.

concepts.title: Shoulder suspension, capsule and stabilizers
concepts.summary: Shoulder stability depends on specific suspensory ligaments, cuff compression and capsular reinforcements. Joint cavities and adjacent bursae define routes for fluid spread.
keyPoints: The coracoid can rotate around a remaining vertical conoid fulcrum. The conoid remains an almost vertical, posteromedial restraint to distraction; loss of the trapezoid permits rotation around it.

Acromioclavicular capsular ligaments damaged with coracoclavicular ligaments preserved. Acromioclavicular ligaments provide the greatest resistance to anteroposterior translation; intact coracoclavicular ligaments retain much of the vertical suspension.
Partition and soft-tissue stability of the sternoclavicular joint. The sternoclavicular disc attaches at these sites, divides the cavity and contributes stability despite limited bony congruence.
Coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments. The rotator interval is the triangular cuff gap reinforced by the coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments.

Filling of the communicating subscapularis bursa can occur without a capsular tear. The anterior opening below the coracoid connects the joint cavity to a bursa around the upper border of subscapularis.
examTraps: Acromioclavicular ligaments chiefly resist anteroposterior displacement; coracoclavicular ligaments chiefly resist vertical translation and rotation.
The rotator interval is a gap between cuff tendons, and the subscapularis bursa can communicate with the joint.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: After an acromioclavicular injury, the trapezoid and acromioclavicular ligaments are torn but the conoid remains intact. Which residual mechanical behavior is most consistent with this pattern?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The coracoid can rotate around a remaining vertical conoid fulcrum. The conoid remains an almost vertical, posteromedial restraint to distraction; loss of the trapezoid permits rotation around it.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: An intra-articular fibrocartilaginous structure is detached from the posterosuperior medial clavicle and from the first costal cartilage near the sternum. Which joint function is most directly compromised?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Partition and soft-tissue stability of the sternoclavicular joint. The sternoclavicular disc attaches at these sites, divides the cavity and contributes stability despite limited bony congruence.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: During a shoulder arthrogram, contrast exits through the normal anterior capsular opening below the coracoid and surrounds the upper border of subscapularis. Which interpretation best fits the anatomy?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Filling of the communicating subscapularis bursa can occur without a capsular tear. The anterior opening below the coracoid connects the joint cavity to a bursa around the upper border of subscapularis.

Distinguish horizontal acromioclavicular instability from failure of vertical coracoclavicular suspension.
Relate sternoclavicular disc attachments to joint partition and stability.
Localize the rotator interval and its ligamentous reinforcements.
Distinguish normal subscapular bursal filling from an abnormal capsular leak.

concepts.title: Branch-level localization in the shoulder and arm
concepts.summary: Selective muscle testing localizes a lesion along the brachial plexus or a terminal nerve. A lesion distal to an early motor branch can spare that muscle while affecting more distal targets.
keyPoints: At the lateral border of the scapular spine after the supraspinatus branches. The nerve supplies supraspinatus before curving around the scapular spine to infraspinatus.
Lower subscapular nerve. The lower subscapular nerve supplies lower subscapularis and usually teres major; separate thoracodorsal and axillary branches remain functional.

Lateral pectoral nerve after it leaves the lateral cord. The lateral pectoral nerve crosses the vessels, pierces clavipectoral fascia and reaches pectoralis major. A distal branch injury spares musculocutaneous function.

Teres minor contraction with sensation over the usual upper lateral cutaneous territory. The posterior axillary branch gives the nerve to teres minor and the upper lateral cutaneous nerve, so these may remain intact.

Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm after the motor branches have arisen. The musculocutaneous nerve continues as this cutaneous branch after supplying arm muscles and passes lateral to the biceps tendon.
examTraps: A distal suprascapular lesion can spare supraspinatus.
Sensory branches and motor branches do not always arise at the same point.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: External rotation is weak and infraspinatus is denervated, but supraspinatus contraction is preserved. Which location best explains an isolated suprascapular neuropathy with this pattern?
retrievalPrompts.answer: At the lateral border of the scapular spine after the supraspinatus branches. The nerve supplies supraspinatus before curving around the scapular spine to infraspinatus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A branch crossing anterior to the axillary vessels is divided where it pierces clavipectoral fascia. Pectoralis major loses part of its innervation, but musculocutaneous motor function remains normal. Which localization is best?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Lateral pectoral nerve after it leaves the lateral cord. The lateral pectoral nerve crosses the vessels, pierces clavipectoral fascia and reaches pectoralis major. A distal branch injury spares musculocutaneous function.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A small penetrating wound lateral to the biceps tendon causes anterolateral forearm numbness. Biceps and brachialis retain normal power. Which structure is most consistent with the lesion?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm after the motor branches have arisen. The musculocutaneous nerve continues as this cutaneous branch after supplying arm muscles and passes lateral to the biceps tendon.

Distinguish lower subscapular injury from neighboring posterior-cord branch injuries.
Use fascial course and spared lateral-cord functions to localize a lateral pectoral lesion.
Distinguish anterior axillary-branch injury from injury of the whole axillary nerve.
Separate distal musculocutaneous sensory injury from proximal motor involvement.

concepts.title: Elbow stability and forearm load transfer
concepts.summary: The radius and ulna function as a linked unit. The radial head, interosseous membrane and distal radioulnar stabilizers share longitudinal loads, while collateral ligaments control angular instability.
keyPoints: Disruption of the interosseous membrane. The radial head, interosseous membrane and distal radioulnar joint are linked longitudinal stabilizers; their combined disruption defines the Essex-Lopresti pattern.
Anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament complex. The anterior ulnar collateral band is the major valgus restraint; an intact complex can maintain stability when the radial head is lost.
Only the outer part of the disc has a substantial blood supply. Gray describes vascularization of approximately the outer 15-20% of the disc, with the remaining central portion avascular.

Radial head spins proximally while the distal radius and hand swing around the ulnar head. The two radioulnar pivot joints act together: proximal radial rotation accompanies a distal arc around the ulna.
Biceps brachii. Biceps contributes especially to rapid or resisted supination in flexion, while supinator can support slow unresisted rotation in extension.
examTraps: A radial-head fracture can be part of a forearm-wide injury.
The central triangular fibrocartilage is much less vascular than its periphery.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A radial-head fracture is accompanied by distal radioulnar instability. Under axial load the radius migrates proximally. Which additional lesion best unifies the findings?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Disruption of the interosseous membrane. The radial head, interosseous membrane and distal radioulnar joint are linked longitudinal stabilizers; their combined disruption defines the Essex-Lopresti pattern.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Two equal-sized tears involve the triangular fibrocartilage: one is central and one peripheral. Why does the central lesion have less intrinsic vascular support for repair?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Only the outer part of the disc has a substantial blood supply. Gray describes vascularization of approximately the outer 15-20% of the disc, with the remaining central portion avascular.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A patient has weak rapid, resisted supination with the elbow flexed, but can still perform slow unresisted supination with the elbow extended. Which muscle's loss best explains the disproportionate deficit?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Biceps brachii. Biceps contributes especially to rapid or resisted supination in flexion, while supinator can support slow unresisted rotation in extension.

Predict valgus instability after combined radial-head and medial ligament failure.
Relate triangular fibrocartilage tear position to its intrinsic vascular repair potential.
Integrate proximal and distal radioulnar movements during pronation.
Use load and elbow position to distinguish contributions to supination.

concepts.title: Forearm vessels and nerve relationships
concepts.summary: Recurrent arteries reconnect distal vessels to the brachial system around the elbow. Fascial openings and muscle heads guide nerves into compartments and explain selective deficits.
keyPoints: Anterior ulnar recurrent artery. It ascends between brachialis and pronator teres to join the inferior ulnar collateral artery anterior to the epicondyle.
Posterior interosseous artery in the posterior forearm. This is the proximal posterior route; the artery accompanies the posterior interosseous nerve among the extensor muscles.
Ulnar head of pronator teres. The median nerve passes between the pronator heads and is separated from the ulnar artery by the ulnar head.

Digital extensors and extensor carpi ulnaris are denervated while proximal radial wrist-extensor branches are spared. The distal deep radial pathway supplies digital extensors and extensor carpi ulnaris. Preserved radial wrist extensors extend the wrist with an unopposed radial component.

A branch of the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm crossing the incision. Branches of this separate cutaneous nerve cross near the cubital-tunnel approach and can be affected without an ulnar motor or digital deficit.
examTraps: A nerve and artery that cross in projection may be separated by a muscle head.
Finger extension can fail while radial wrist extension remains.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Contrast in the inferior ulnar collateral artery crosses to the ulnar arterial system anterior to the medial epicondyle. Which returning branch completes this direct anastomosis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Anterior ulnar recurrent artery. It ascends between brachialis and pronator teres to join the inferior ulnar collateral artery anterior to the epicondyle.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: The median nerve crosses superficial to the ulnar artery in the proximal forearm. What usually lies between these two structures at their crossing?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Ulnar head of pronator teres. The median nerve passes between the pronator heads and is separated from the ulnar artery by the ulnar head.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: After an operation near the cubital tunnel, finger abduction and ulnar digital sensation remain normal, but a patch of medial forearm skin is numb. Which injury best explains this selective new deficit?
retrievalPrompts.answer: A branch of the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm crossing the incision. Branches of this separate cutaneous nerve cross near the cubital-tunnel approach and can be affected without an ulnar motor or digital deficit.

concepts.title: Finger and thumb tendon mechanics
concepts.summary: The extensor expansion, volar plates and flexor pulleys couple motion across finger joints. Their failure produces distinct deformities even when the main muscle and nerve remain intact.
keyPoints: Terminal extensor disruption allows proximal migration of the extensor apparatus, increasing its PIP extension moment. A mallet lesion removes distal restraint. The remaining extensor apparatus can migrate proximally and contribute to secondary swan-neck deformity.

Palmar migration of the lateral bands past the PIP axis after central-slip failure. With central-slip failure and attenuation of the triangular ligament, the lateral bands move volarly; they flex the PIP while the tightened terminal mechanism still extends the DIP.

The adductor aponeurosis is interposed between the avulsed ligament and its distal attachment. A Stener lesion displaces the torn ligament around the free edge of the adductor aponeurosis, which prevents apposition to its insertion.
A2 and A4. A2 overlies the proximal phalanx and A4 the middle phalanx; these are the key finger pulleys resisting flexor bowstringing.

The wider palmar metacarpal head tightens MCP collateral ligaments in flexion, while PIP proper collaterals stay taut throughout motion. The changing metacarpal-head width gives position-dependent MCP collateral tension; PIP collateral restraint is maintained through flexion and extension.
examTraps: Mallet and boutonniere deformities arise at different levels of the extensor apparatus.
Digit MCP collateral ligaments tighten in flexion; PIP collaterals remain taut across the movement arc.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Following forced flexion of an extended fingertip, active DIP extension is lost but passive extension is full. Months later the PIP joint hyperextends. What sequence best explains the progression?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Terminal extensor disruption allows proximal migration of the extensor apparatus, increasing its PIP extension moment. A mallet lesion removes distal restraint. The remaining extensor apparatus can migrate proximally and contribute to secondary swan-neck deformity.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: After forced radial deviation of the thumb MCP joint, its torn ulnar collateral ligament lies superficial to the adductor aponeurosis. Why is direct ligament healing impeded?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The adductor aponeurosis is interposed between the avulsed ligament and its distal attachment. A Stener lesion displaces the torn ligament around the free edge of the adductor aponeurosis, which prevents apposition to its insertion.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: An intact finger allows lateral movement at the MCP joint in extension but very little when that joint is fully flexed. The PIP remains stable in both positions. Which explanation best fits?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The wider palmar metacarpal head tightens MCP collateral ligaments in flexion, while PIP proper collaterals stay taut throughout motion. The changing metacarpal-head width gives position-dependent MCP collateral tension; PIP collateral restraint is maintained through flexion and extension.

concepts.title: Hand nerve branches, arches and tendon sheaths
concepts.summary: Hand symptoms depend on whether a lesion affects proximal or distal branches, and infections follow specific synovial sheaths. Palmar arches and tendon nutrient folds occupy different depths.
keyPoints: Deep ulnar branch after its hypothenar muscular branches. The deep branch gives hypothenar branches near its origin before crossing to the interossei and adductor pollicis; superficial sensory and palmaris-brevis fibers remain separate.

The corresponding dorsal distal phalanx and nail-bed region. Proper palmar digital branches extend dorsally to supply distal finger skin; proximal dorsal and distal dorsal territories do not have identical sources.
Into the common digital-flexor sheath at the wrist. The little-finger sheath usually continues into the common sheath surrounding FDS and FDP through the carpal tunnel.
Delivery of blood vessels through the vincula. Vincula are specialized synovial folds carrying vessels to gliding flexor tendons, including short folds near the insertions.
Deep palmar arch. The deep palmar arch lies deep to flexor tendons and lumbricals, on the bases of the metacarpals and interossei, accompanying the deep ulnar branch.
examTraps: Dorsal fingertip sensation can come from a palmar digital nerve.
The little-finger sheath usually communicates proximally; the middle three digital sheaths usually end separately.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A small deep palmar lesion causes interosseous and adductor-pollicis weakness, but hypothenar muscle function, palmaris brevis and ulnar digital sensation remain intact. Which site best fits?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Deep ulnar branch after its hypothenar muscular branches. The deep branch gives hypothenar branches near its origin before crossing to the interossei and adductor pollicis; superficial sensory and palmaris-brevis fibers remain separate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: An infection begins within the little-finger flexor synovial sheath. Which proximal route is anatomically most likely in the usual arrangement?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Into the common digital-flexor sheath at the wrist. The little-finger sheath usually continues into the common sheath surrounding FDS and FDP through the carpal tunnel.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: During a palmar dissection, the digital flexor tendons and lumbricals are lifted. An arterial arch lies against the metacarpal bases and interossei with the deep ulnar nerve in its concavity. Which structure is exposed?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Deep palmar arch. The deep palmar arch lies deep to flexor tendons and lumbricals, on the bases of the metacarpals and interossei, accompanying the deep ulnar branch.

concepts.title: Hip capsule, cartilage and communicating spaces
concepts.summary: The capsule has asymmetric femoral attachments and contains the capital growth plate. The acetabular articular ring, central fossa and adjacent bursae explain loading and fluid distribution.
keyPoints: Posterior attachment is proximal to the crest; anterior attachment reaches the intertrochanteric line. The capsule attaches posteriorly about 1 cm superomedial to the crest but anteriorly at the intertrochanteric line.

The position increases capsular capacity and reduces tension from wound-up capsular ligaments. Hip capacity is maximal in partial flexion and abduction; extension winds the capsule and raises restraint.

The anterosuperior lunate surface bears substantial load, while the central acetabular fossa is nonarticular. The lunate articular surface is widest and cartilage thickest where body weight is transmitted; the fossa contains fibroelastic fat.
Iliopectineal bursa. This bursa can communicate with the hip joint through the specified anterior capsular interval.

The physis is avascular, so retinacular vessels must reach the head around its edge. The capital epiphysis is intracapsular and separated by an avascular plate; retinacular vessels passing around its edge are crucial to head perfusion.
examTraps: The acetabular fossa is nonarticular despite lying centrally in the socket.
Hip capsular capacity is greatest with partial flexion and abduction, whereas extension tightens the capsule.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A surgeon exposes the posterior femoral neck near the intertrochanteric crest. Which comparison with the anterior attachment of the hip capsule is correct?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Posterior attachment is proximal to the crest; anterior attachment reaches the intertrochanteric line. The capsule attaches posteriorly about 1 cm superomedial to the crest but anteriorly at the intertrochanteric line.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A specimen shows thick hyaline cartilage on the anterosuperior acetabular ring, but fat and synovium in its central depression. Which functional interpretation is correct?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The anterosuperior lunate surface bears substantial load, while the central acetabular fossa is nonarticular. The lunate articular surface is widest and cartilage thickest where body weight is transmitted; the fossa contains fibroelastic fat.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: In an adolescent, injury crosses the capital femoral growth plate. Why can the head's circulation be endangered even when vessels within the neck remain patent below the growth plate?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The physis is avascular, so retinacular vessels must reach the head around its edge. The capital epiphysis is intracapsular and separated by an avascular plate; retinacular vessels passing around its edge are crucial to head perfusion.

concepts.title: Thigh circulation and changing neurovascular planes
concepts.summary: The profunda femoris and its perforating branches form longitudinal collateral channels, while the femoral vein changes sides along the artery. Superficial venous and cutaneous nerve routes explain selective procedural deficits.
keyPoints: Medial proximally and posterolateral distally. The vein lies medial at the triangle base, posterior near the apex and posterolateral in the distal adductor canal.

Inferior gluteal artery to the first perforating and circumflex femoral anastomoses. The gluteal-circumflex-perforating connections can reach the profunda system distal to a proximal femoral obstruction.

Profunda perforators anastomose with one another and with gluteal and popliteal muscular branches at the ends. The perforators cross the adductor attachment and form a linked posterior thigh chain from gluteal to popliteal territories.
Saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery. This branch accompanies the saphenous nerve through the canal roof toward the medial knee and proximal leg.
Injury of the cutaneous saphenous nerve accompanying the vein in the leg. The saphenous nerve travels with the great saphenous vein in the leg and supplies skin without motor innervation.
examTraps: The femoral vein is medial at the triangle base but posterolateral in the distal adductor canal.
A patent collateral connection must enter the circulation downstream of an occlusion.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Two transverse images are obtained: one at the base of the femoral triangle and one at the distal adductor canal. Where is the femoral vein expected relative to its artery at these two levels?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Medial proximally and posterolateral distally. The vein lies medial at the triangle base, posterior near the apex and posterolateral in the distal adductor canal.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A posterior thigh exposure identifies arteries passing through tendinous arches in adductor magnus near the linea aspera. Which arrangement explains their ability to distribute blood longitudinally?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Profunda perforators anastomose with one another and with gluteal and popliteal muscular branches at the ends. The perforators cross the adductor attachment and form a linked posterior thigh chain from gluteal to popliteal territories.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Following harvesting of the great saphenous vein in the leg, a patient develops medial leg numbness but normal quadriceps strength and foot movements. Which explanation best fits?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Injury of the cutaneous saphenous nerve accompanying the vein in the leg. The saphenous nerve travels with the great saphenous vein in the leg and supplies skin without motor innervation.

concepts.title: Knee recesses, stabilizers and load-bearing mechanics
concepts.summary: Knee fluid follows synovial recesses, while flexion changes cruciate tension, patellar restraint and the muscular work required to support body weight.
keyPoints: Articularis genus. Articularis genus retracts the suprapatellar bursa/recess during extension, helping prevent synovial tissue from being caught.
The gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa. This posteromedial bursa may communicate with the knee and form a typical Baker cyst.

Reduced posterior restraint in flexion, when the anterolateral bundle normally becomes taut. The PCL anterolateral bundle is tight in flexion; the posteromedial bundle is preferentially tight in extension.

The body-weight line moves behind the knee axis, creating a flexion moment that quadriceps must oppose. In a flexed weight-bearing knee, the line of body weight passes behind the joint axis; sustained quadriceps activity prevents further flexion.
The medial patellofemoral ligament and medial quadriceps contribution. Trochlear geometry and medial soft-tissue restraints oppose the tendency of the patella to displace laterally.
examTraps: The suprapatellar recess is continuous with the knee cavity, whereas a typical popliteal cyst occupies the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa.
Flexing a weight-bearing knee increases the need for active quadriceps support.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A large knee effusion extends superiorly deep to quadriceps. During knee extension, which small muscle normally pulls the wall of this communicating recess away from the moving joint?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Articularis genus. Articularis genus retracts the suprapatellar bursa/recess during extension, helping prevent synovial tissue from being caught.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A reconstruction is being assessed separately in knee flexion and extension. The anterolateral bundle of the posterior cruciate ligament has failed, while the posteromedial bundle is intact. Which mechanical deficit is most directly expected?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Reduced posterior restraint in flexion, when the anterolateral bundle normally becomes taut. The PCL anterolateral bundle is tight in flexion; the posteromedial bundle is preferentially tight in extension.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Recurrent lateral patellar displacement occurs in a knee with a shallow lateral trochlear wall. Loss of which additional restraint would most compound the deficient bony guidance?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The medial patellofemoral ligament and medial quadriceps contribution. Trochlear geometry and medial soft-tissue restraints oppose the tendency of the patella to displace laterally.

concepts.title: Localizing leg nerve lesions by spared functions
concepts.summary: Distinguish nerve injury levels by combining cutaneous loss with motor functions supplied before and after the suspected lesion.
keyPoints: Tibialis posterior receives L5 fibers through the tibial nerve and is spared by the local common fibular lesion. The spared inverter samples L5 motor function outside the common fibular nerve; a broader L5 lesion may also weaken it.

The common fibular component of the sciatic nerve proximal to its short-head branch. The short head of biceps receives the common fibular division above the fibular neck; its involvement places the lesion proximal to that branch, while tibial-division muscles are spared.

Compression of the distal deep fibular nerve after its branches to the anterior leg muscles. The distal nerve supplies the first web space and short extensors after proximal motor branches have already departed.
The branches to fibularis longus and brevis arise before the nerve becomes superficial. A distal cutaneous injury occurs beyond the motor supply to the lateral compartment.

Both weak muscles receive tibial motor branches in the leg, proximal to the tarsal tunnel. A distal tunnel lesion cannot account for denervation of these proximal extrinsic muscles; a more proximal lesion or additional pathology is needed.
examTraps: Preserved tibialis posterior separates a common fibular lesion from a broader L5-pattern lesion.
The distal deep fibular nerve cannot explain loss of proximal anterior-compartment function.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: After compression at the fibular neck, a patient has weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion. Inversion against resistance remains strong when tested with the ankle slightly plantarflexed. Why does this pattern favor a common fibular neuropathy over an L5 root lesion?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Tibialis posterior receives L5 fibers through the tibial nerve and is spared by the local common fibular lesion. The spared inverter samples L5 motor function outside the common fibular nerve; a broader L5 lesion may also weaken it.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A tight strap at the anterior ankle is followed by first-web-space numbness and weakness of extensor digitorum brevis. Ankle dorsiflexion and long-toe extension are normal. Which explanation best fits?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Compression of the distal deep fibular nerve after its branches to the anterior leg muscles. The distal nerve supplies the first web space and short extensors after proximal motor branches have already departed.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A patient referred for presumed tarsal-tunnel compression has plantar sensory loss, but also clear weakness of tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus. Which finding challenges a lesion confined behind the medial malleolus?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Both weak muscles receive tibial motor branches in the leg, proximal to the tarsal tunnel. A distal tunnel lesion cannot account for denervation of these proximal extrinsic muscles; a more proximal lesion or additional pathology is needed.

concepts.title: Ankle mortise, tendon restraints and surgical relations
concepts.summary: The ankle mortise accommodates the asymmetric talar trochlea; retinacula restrain tendons along different routes from the collateral ligaments.
keyPoints: Slight separation and adjustment of the malleoli as the broader anterior talar trochlea enters the mortise. The trochlea is wider anteriorly; dorsiflexion requires the mortise to accommodate that wider region through small tibiofibular movements.
Disruption of the superior fibular retinaculum. The superior fibular retinaculum holds these tendons in the retromalleolar groove; its failure permits subluxation.

The tibial nerve and posterior tibial vessels lie medially to flexor hallucis longus. Flexor hallucis longus is a surgical landmark separating a lateral working interval from the medial neurovascular bundle.
Fibularis longus. An os peroneum may lie within fibularis longus near its cuboid turn; displacement can accompany tendon injury.

Anterior tibial artery at its transition to dorsalis pedis, and deep fibular nerve. At this level the anterior tibial artery lies lateral to extensor hallucis longus, with the deep fibular nerve lateral to the artery.
examTraps: Tendon subluxation behind the lateral malleolus points to a fibular retinaculum, not simply the anterior talofibular ligament.
At the posterior ankle the neurovascular bundle is medial to flexor hallucis longus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: A healed distal tibiofibular fusion leaves normal talocrural cartilage but restricts end-range dorsiflexion. Which normal geometric accommodation has been lost?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Slight separation and adjustment of the malleoli as the broader anterior talar trochlea enters the mortise. The trochlea is wider anteriorly; dorsiflexion requires the mortise to accommodate that wider region through small tibiofibular movements.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: During a posterior ankle dissection, the flexor hallucis longus muscle-tendon unit is identified. A working interval is maintained on its lateral side. Which important relationship makes that interval protective?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The tibial nerve and posterior tibial vessels lie medially to flexor hallucis longus. Flexor hallucis longus is a surgical landmark separating a lateral working interval from the medial neurovascular bundle.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: At the anterior ankle a needle is placed immediately lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. Arterial pulsation is encountered, and a neighboring nerve lies lateral to that artery. Which artery-nerve pair fits this arrangement?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Anterior tibial artery at its transition to dorsalis pedis, and deep fibular nerve. At this level the anterior tibial artery lies lateral to extensor hallucis longus, with the deep fibular nerve lateral to the artery.

concepts.title: Foot arches, intrinsic mechanics and deep circulation
concepts.summary: Passive fascial tension and intrinsic muscle lines of pull shape the foot as a lever, while plantar nerve branches and vascular arches occupy distinct tissue planes.
keyPoints: The plantar aponeurosis winds around the metatarsal head and draws the arch's pillars together. Metatarsophalangeal extension tensions the aponeurosis through the windlass mechanism, raising the arch passively.

Redirection of the long flexor's oblique pull to assist straight flexion of the lateral four toes. Quadratus plantae attaches to the long flexor tendons and helps correct their oblique line of traction.
Flexor hallucis brevis weakness. The medial plantar nerve supplies abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and the first lumbrical.

The deep plantar branch of dorsalis pedis entering through the first intermetatarsal space. The lateral plantar artery forms the deep arch, completed medially by the deep plantar continuation from dorsalis pedis.

Flexor hallucis longus continuing between the sesamoids to the distal phalanx. The sesamoids lie in the two flexor hallucis brevis tendons, while flexor hallucis longus continues distally and can flex the interphalangeal joint.
examTraps: Great-toe extension can raise the arch passively through the plantar aponeurosis.
Flexor hallucis brevis acts at the first metatarsophalangeal joint; flexor hallucis longus remains capable of interphalangeal flexion.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: While the foot remains weight-bearing, an examiner passively extends the great toe. The medial longitudinal arch rises even without voluntary intrinsic-muscle contraction. Which mechanism best explains this?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The plantar aponeurosis winds around the metatarsal head and draws the arch's pillars together. Metatarsophalangeal extension tensions the aponeurosis through the windlass mechanism, raising the arch passively.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: After a focal medial plantar nerve injury, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and the first lumbrical are weak. Which additional weakness belongs to the same motor territory rather than implying lateral plantar involvement?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Flexor hallucis brevis weakness. The medial plantar nerve supplies abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and the first lumbrical.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: After loss of both first-metatarsophalangeal sesamoids and their attached short-flexor tendon insertions, a patient has weak flexion at that joint but can still actively flex the hallux interphalangeal joint. Which preserved structure explains the latter movement?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Flexor hallucis longus continuing between the sesamoids to the distal phalanx. The sesamoids lie in the two flexor hallucis brevis tendons, while flexor hallucis longus continues distally and can flex the interphalangeal joint.

concepts.title: Limb growth, compartment innervation and developmental disruptions
concepts.summary: Limb elongation, muscle innervation and congenital deformities arise through different developmental processes. Distinguishing loss of growth, altered pattern and reduced fetal movement clarifies otherwise similar limb findings.
keyPoints: Loss of length contribution from that growth plate despite continued possible appositional growth and remodeling. Longitudinal growth depends on proliferating growth-plate cartilage; an intact shaft and periosteum cannot restore the lost plate's contribution to length.

Dorsal divisions of the ventral primary rami entering the brachial plexus. The limb muscle compartments receive branches of ventral primary rami; those rami divide into dorsal and ventral divisions within the developing plexus.
HOXA13 in the first family; HOXD13 in the second. Langman associates HOXA13 mutations with hand-foot-genital syndrome and HOXD13 mutations with synpolydactyly.

The first disrupts initiation of outgrowth; the second disrupts maintenance of the adjacent proliferating undifferentiated zone. FGF10 from lateral plate mesoderm initiates outgrowth, whereas ridge-derived FGF4 and FGF8 support continued proliferation after ridge establishment.

Restricted fetal movement can produce arthrogryposis despite formation of the skeletal elements. Intrauterine crowding and reduced movement are recognized routes to congenital joint contractures, distinct from failure to form the limb rays.
examTraps: Dorsal limb muscle masses receive dorsal divisions of ventral primary rami, not dorsal primary rami.
A contracted but formed joint need not reflect failure of the early digit-patterning system.

concepts.title: Cartilage resilience and bone mechanobiology
concepts.summary: Limb tissues share connective-tissue ancestry but have distinct nutrient routes and mechanical components. Cartilage hydration, osteocyte sensing and osteoclast resorption explain functional and disease patterns.
keyPoints: Fixed negative charges that retain water within the collagen-proteoglycan network. Sulfated GAGs and hyaluronan bind water; this hydrated network gives cartilage much of its compressive resilience.

Articular chondrocytes depend on diffusion from synovial fluid, whereas osteocytes use the lacunar-canalicular fluid network connected to nearby vessels. Articular cartilage lacks vessels and perichondrium; bone cells communicate and exchange metabolites through canaliculi linked to vascularized bone surfaces.

Osteocyte processes in canaliculi connected by gap junctions to a wider bone-cell network. The lacunar-canalicular network allows osteocytes to detect load and microdamage and signal osteoblast and osteoclast responses.

Failure of osteoclast proton transport or supporting chloride conductance, impairing mineral resorption. Defective acidification impairs removal of hydroxyapatite; excess retained bone can narrow marrow cavities and reduce blood-cell production.

Mineral confers hardness, while the collagen framework contributes shape and resilience under load. Decalcification leaves an organic collagen framework; collagen defects remove reinforcement and resilience even when mineral is present.
examTraps: Dense bone can be fragile and can compromise marrow space when osteoclast resorption fails.
Mineral supplies hardness while the type I collagen framework contributes resilience; they are not interchangeable.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Fixed negative charges that retain water within the collagen-proteoglycan network. Sulfated GAGs and hyaluronan bind water; this hydrated network gives cartilage much of its compressive resilience.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Osteocyte processes in canaliculi connected by gap junctions to a wider bone-cell network. The lacunar-canalicular network allows osteocytes to detect load and microdamage and signal osteoblast and osteoclast responses.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Mineral confers hardness, while the collagen framework contributes shape and resilience under load. Decalcification leaves an organic collagen framework; collagen defects remove reinforcement and resilience even when mineral is present.

concepts.title: Muscle force transmission, excitation architecture and repair
concepts.summary: A skeletal muscle is a mechanically continuous tissue whose fibers transmit force through collagen. Sarcomeric accessory proteins, triads and satellite cells solve distinct structural problems.
keyPoints: Endomysial, perimysial and epimysial collagen form a continuous force-transmitting network with tendon. Connective-tissue sheaths transmit force from individual fibers and are continuous with tendon at myotendinous junctions.
Titin. Titin provides elastic and scaffolding support linking thick filaments with the Z disc; the spared thin-filament features argue against the other listed proteins.

A surface-connected T tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum. The central T tubule is an invagination of sarcolemma continuous with the extracellular compartment; the two flanking SR cisternae are separate intracellular calcium stores.

Activation of satellite cells to generate or contribute to skeletal muscle fibers. Satellite cells persist as reserve myogenic cells inside the external lamina and can proliferate and fuse after injury.

Hypertrophy of existing skeletal muscle fibers. The specified increase in cell size and contractile material is hypertrophy; satellite-cell contribution may accompany growth but is not evidence that mature fibers divide.
examTraps: A T tubule is an invagination of the surface membrane, not a sarcoplasmic-reticulum cistern.
Mature multinucleated skeletal fibers do not divide to repair injury; satellite cells provide limited regeneration.

concepts.title: Skeletal-muscle length, load, activation and relaxation
concepts.summary: Separating active from passive tension, force from shortening, and electrical excitation from calcium handling explains muscle behavior under experimental and limb-loading conditions.
keyPoints: Active tension fell from 8 N to 5 N even though total tension increased. Active tension is total stimulated tension minus passive tension: 10-2=8 N and 12-7=5 N. Increasing passive stretch can mask a decline in cross-bridge-generated tension.

External shortening work is zero, but ATP use and heat production can continue. At a load equal to maximal isometric force, shortening velocity is zero; external work requires displacement, whereas active force maintenance still uses metabolic energy.

Calcium remains elevated between stimuli, allowing successive mechanical responses to summate. When stimuli recur before calcium is fully resequestered and tension relaxes, mechanical responses summate and can form a fused tetanus.

The end-plate depolarization no longer reaches the threshold for a muscle action potential. Receptor blockade reduces the end-plate potential; preserved direct excitability and contraction locate the deficit at neuromuscular transmission rather than the muscle's contractile apparatus.

The sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium ATPase responsible for resequestration. Reduced SR calcium pumping delays removal of cytosolic calcium, prolonging activation and relaxation despite preserved initial excitation and release.
examTraps: No external shortening does not mean no ATP use or force production.
Fused mechanical tension is not fusion of muscle action potentials; delayed relaxation differs from failed excitation.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Calcium remains elevated between stimuli, allowing successive mechanical responses to summate. When stimuli recur before calcium is fully resequestered and tension relaxes, mechanical responses summate and can form a fused tetanus.

retrievalPrompts.answer: The sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium ATPase responsible for resequestration. Reduced SR calcium pumping delays removal of cytosolic calcium, prolonging activation and relaxation despite preserved initial excitation and release.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Upper limb bones and landmarks
concepts.summary: Name and locate the labeled anatomy in Upper limb bones and landmarks. Follow each original callout to its structure and explain its anatomical relationships. Reverse practice uses the authored callout boxes rather than pretending the whole structure is pixel-segmented. A hook-shaped projection from the superior scapula, lying anterior to the glenoid and serving as an attachment for muscles and ligaments.
keyPoints: Coracoid process: A hook-shaped projection from the superior scapula, lying anterior to the glenoid and serving as an attachment for muscles and ligaments.
Superior angle: The superior angle is where the superior and medial borders of the scapula meet.
Acromion: The acromion continues laterally from the scapular spine and forms the bony roof above the shoulder joint.
Clavicle: An S-shaped subcutaneous strut between the manubrium and acromion that holds the upper limb away from the trunk and transmits load to the axial skeleton.
Intertubercular groove: The groove between the greater and lesser humeral tubercles contains the tendon of the long head of biceps.
Surgical neck: The surgical neck is the narrowed region below the humeral tubercles, close to the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.
Lesser tubercle: The lesser tubercle projects anteriorly from the proximal humerus and receives the subscapularis tendon.
Greater tubercle: The greater tubercle is the lateral prominence of the proximal humerus and receives supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor.
Medial epicondyle: The medial epicondyle projects from the distal humerus and gives origin to the common superficial flexor group.
Lateral epicondyle: The lateral epicondyle projects from the distal humerus and gives origin to the common extensor tendon.
Trochlea: The spool-shaped humeral trochlea articulates with the trochlear notch of the ulna at the elbow.
Coronoid process: The coronoid process forms the anterior projection of the proximal ulna below the trochlear notch.
Deltoid tuberosity: The deltoid tuberosity is a rough lateral shaft prominence that receives the deltoid insertion.
Humerus: The long bone of the arm, articulating with the glenoid proximally and the radius and ulna distally; key landmarks include the surgical neck, radial groove and medial epicondyle.
Ulna: The medial forearm bone, whose olecranon and coronoid process form the trochlear notch around the humeral trochlea; its distal head is separated from the carpus by an articular disc.
Ulna, styloid process: The ulnar styloid process projects distally from the posteromedial aspect of the ulnar head.
Radius, styloid process: The radial styloid process projects distally from the lateral radius on the thumb side of the wrist.
Carpal bones: Eight short bones arranged in proximal and distal rows form the carpus between the forearm and metacarpals.
Radius: The lateral forearm bone in anatomical position, with a disc-shaped head proximally and a broad distal end that articulates with the scaphoid and lunate.
Scapula: A triangular flat bone on the posterolateral thoracic wall, spanning roughly ribs 2–7; its lateral angle bears the glenoid cavity and its spine expands into the acromion.
Inferior angle: The inferior angle is the meeting point of the medial and lateral scapular borders.
Tuberosity of radius: The radial tuberosity lies just distal to the radial neck and receives the biceps brachii tendon.
Capitulum: The rounded lateral articular surface of the distal humerus articulates with the head of the radius.
Head of radius: The disc-shaped radial head articulates with the capitulum and rotates within the annular ligament.
examTraps: Follow the complete leader line to its endpoint; a nearby structure can be a plausible distractor.
Check the viewing direction and laterality before naming a structure. The 3D view may show the other side of the same anatomical relationship.
