concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Brachial plexus in anatomical context
concepts.summary: Name and locate the labeled anatomy in Brachial plexus in anatomical context. Follow each original callout to its structure and explain its anatomical relationships. Reverse practice uses the authored callout boxes rather than pretending the whole structure is pixel-segmented. The C5 ventral ramus emerges between the anterior and middle scalene muscles and joins C6 to form the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.
keyPoints: C5 root of brachial plexus: The C5 ventral ramus emerges between the anterior and middle scalene muscles and joins C6 to form the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.
C6 root of brachial plexus: The C6 ventral ramus passes through the interscalene interval and joins C5 to complete the upper trunk.
C7 root of brachial plexus: The C7 ventral ramus continues by itself as the middle trunk before dividing behind the clavicle.
C8 root of brachial plexus: The C8 ventral ramus ascends over the first rib to join T1 and form the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.
T1 root of brachial plexus: Most of the T1 ventral ramus joins C8 above the first rib to form the lower trunk; a smaller part remains as the first intercostal nerve.
Dorsal scapular nerve: A branch usually arising from the C5 root that pierces middle scalene and descends along the medial border of the scapula with the dorsal scapular artery.
Upper trunk of brachial plexus: The union of the C5 and C6 ventral rami at the lateral border of the scalene interval, dividing into anterior and posterior divisions above the clavicle.
Middle trunk of brachial plexus: The continuation of the C7 ventral ramus through the interscalene interval, dividing into anterior and posterior divisions behind the clavicle.
Lower trunk of brachial plexus: The union of C8 and T1 ventral rami, lying inferiorly in the plexus before dividing behind the clavicle.
Medial cord of brachial plexus: A cord medial to the second part of the axillary artery, formed by the anterior division of the lower trunk.
Lateral cord of brachial plexus: A cord lateral to the second part of the axillary artery, formed by the anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks.
Posterior cord of brachial plexus: A cord posterior to the second part of the axillary artery, formed by all three posterior divisions.
Suprascapular nerve: A branch of the upper trunk that crosses the posterior triangle and passes under the superior transverse scapular ligament into the supraspinous fossa.
Lateral pectoral nerve: A branch of the lateral cord that crosses anterior to the axillary artery, pierces clavipectoral fascia and chiefly supplies pectoralis major.
Medial pectoral nerve: A branch of the medial cord that typically pierces pectoralis minor and continues into the deep surface of pectoralis major.
Axillary artery: The continuation of the subclavian from the lateral border of the first rib to the inferior border of teres major, where it becomes brachial.

Musculocutaneous nerve: A C5–C7 terminal branch of the lateral cord that pierces coracobrachialis and descends between biceps and brachialis before continuing as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
Axillary nerve: A C5–C6 terminal branch of the posterior cord that passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery and winds around the surgical neck.
Median nerve: A terminal nerve formed by lateral and medial roots around the axillary artery, descending with the brachial artery and entering the hand through the carpal tunnel.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate Tuberosity of navicular and describe its relationship to surrounding structures.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The navicular tuberosity projects medially and receives the main tibialis posterior tendon attachment.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate Long plantar ligament and describe its relationship to surrounding structures.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The long plantar ligament runs from the plantar calcaneus toward the cuboid and metatarsal bases, supporting the lateral longitudinal arch.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate Plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament and describe its relationship to surrounding structures.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The spring ligament spans the sustentaculum tali and navicular and supports the head of the talus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate Sustentaculum tali and describe its relationship to surrounding structures.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The sustentaculum tali is the medial calcaneal shelf supporting the talus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate Superficial parts of deltoid ligament and describe its relationship to surrounding structures.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The superficial deltoid ligament fans from the medial malleolus toward the navicular, calcaneus and talus, reinforcing the medial ankle.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate Anterior tibiofibular ligament and describe its relationship to surrounding structures.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The anterior tibiofibular ligament strengthens the front of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate Anterior talofibular ligament and describe its relationship to surrounding structures.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The anterior talofibular ligament links the anterior lateral malleolus to the talar neck.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate Bifurcate ligament and describe its relationship to surrounding structures.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The bifurcate ligament arises from the anterior calcaneus and divides toward the navicular and cuboid.

concepts.title: Plantar nerves and vessels between muscle layers
concepts.summary: Name and locate the labeled anatomy in Plantar nerves and vessels between muscle layers. Follow each original callout to its structure and explain its anatomical relationships. Reverse practice uses the authored callout boxes rather than pretending the whole structure is pixel-segmented. The common plantar digital nerves run forward in the sole and divide into proper digital branches for adjacent toes.
keyPoints: Common plantar digital nerves: The common plantar digital nerves run forward in the sole and divide into proper digital branches for adjacent toes.
Lateral plantar artery: The larger terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery that crosses the lateral sole and turns medially to form most of the deep plantar arch.
Abductor digiti minimi: In the foot, abductor digiti minimi occupies the lateral sole and inserts on the lateral side of the fifth toe proximal phalanx.
Plantar aponeurosis: The plantar aponeurosis runs from the calcaneal tuberosity toward the toes and supports the longitudinal arch.
Lateral plantar nerve: The smaller tibial terminal branch runs obliquely across the sole with the lateral plantar artery and divides into superficial and deep branches.
Posterior tibial artery: This terminal branch of the popliteal artery descends in the deep posterior compartment and passes behind the medial malleolus into the sole.
Flexor retinaculum: The ankle flexor retinaculum extends from the medial malleolus to the calcaneus and roofs the tarsal tunnel.
Medial plantar nerve: The larger tibial terminal branch runs forward in the sole with the medial plantar artery between abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis.
Flexor accessorius: Flexor accessorius, also called quadratus plantae, arises from the calcaneus and joins the flexor digitorum longus tendons.
Abductor hallucis: Abductor hallucis occupies the medial margin of the sole and inserts on the medial side of the hallux proximal phalanx.
Flexor hallucis brevis: Flexor hallucis brevis is a short plantar muscle whose two heads insert on either side of the base of the hallux proximal phalanx.
Flexor digitorum brevis: Flexor digitorum brevis lies in the first plantar muscle layer and sends divided tendons to the middle phalanges of toes two through five.
examTraps: Follow the complete leader line to its endpoint; a nearby structure can be a plausible distractor.
Check the viewing direction and laterality before naming a structure. The 3D view may show the other side of the same anatomical relationship.
